title: How OpenFlows compares
summary: Every AI tool writes code. They differ in where the human sits . OpenFlows is a self& 8209;hosted, governed, agent& 8209;first team - not a chat assistant, not a hosted autonomous…
text: How OpenFlows compares Every AI tool writes code. They differ in where the human sits . OpenFlows is a self& 8209;hosted, governed, agent& 8209;first team - not a chat assistant, not a hosted autonomous coder, and not a bare orchestrator. AI writes code faster than any team can consume it, so review - not writing - is the bottleneck . The first pass of that review must be done by another agent before a human ever sees anything, and OpenFlows moves humans up the chain to architecture and product ownership. This page compares that to the alternatives. Every AI tool writes code - they differ in where the human sits. Where humans sit in the pipeline Anything that writes code for a human to review Intake Plan Build Test Review ⛔ human Merge Ship Throughput collapses to review speed. OpenFlows Human - architecture product Intake NEXUS Plan FORGE Build FORGE Test FORGE Review SENTINEL only decisions reach the human Merge VESSEL Ship Only decisions reach the human. Humans move from the bottleneck to the helm. The position map human& 8209;gated & 10625; agent& 8209;first OpenFlows Bare orchestrator your infra, agent& 8209;first bare = you build it their cloud, agent& 8209;first Chat assistant your infra, human& 8209;gated Hosted autonomous coder their cloud, human& 8209;gated ◀ your infrastructure & 8226; their cloud ▶ OpenFlows is the only one that is both on your infrastructure and agent& 8209;first - you get governance and throughput. The short version The trade-offs, one by one OpenFlows vs. a coding chat assistant Both are powered by language models writing code. The difference is process - and whether the human is the bottleneck. Chat assistants are a tool you operate. You prompt, you review, you accept. Because the assistant can write code faster than you can review it, you become the limiting step - every change funnels through your judgment, so the pipeline slows back down to human speed and costs you hours of accept& 8209;or& 8209;deny clicking. OpenFlows is a team that operates itself. It plans before coding, gives every change a first& 8209;pass review by another agent , and escalates to you only for genuine decisions - so you move up the chain to architecture and product, not down into the review queue. Best for: when you want AI to execute end& 8209;to& 8209;end with guardrails, not just help you type. OpenFlows vs. a hosted autonomous coder Both automate coding end& 8209;to& 8209;end. The difference is where it runs and who can audit it. Hosted agents run in their cloud. Code, prompts, and outputs leave your network; you rely on their security and their review process, and you cannot fully audit. OpenFlows can be self-hosted. Manager and Coder run in your infrastructure; Manager holds long-lived platform secrets and brokers scoped runtime credentials to workspaces. Review your model provider and GitHub data paths as part of deployment. Best for: regulated companies and anyone who cannot or will not send code to a third& 8209;party cloud. OpenFlows vs. a bare orchestrator Both automate a multi& 8209;step agent pipeline. The difference is how much you build and maintain. A bare orchestrator gives you a flow that you author and debug yourself - routing, retries, state, and recovery are all your responsibility. OpenFlows ships the coordination as a product: a typed shared store, a gated planning cycle, adversarial review, self& 8209;healing reconciliation, and human escalation - all already built. Best for: teams that want the engineering of the coordination handled, not reinvented. OpenFlows vs. Coder alone Coder is the substrate; OpenFlows is what runs on it. Coder alone gives you governed, disposable workspaces and a model gateway - an excellent place for humans to work. OpenFlows adds the team. It provisions those workspaces, assigns one agent per ticket, coordinates their hand& 8209;offs, and drives the work to a reviewed merge. In OpenFlows' own framing: Coder governs where agents run; OpenFlows governs how they coordinate. This separation is the whole architecture. Where the time goes Classic assistant workflow Accept / Deny per change Architecture thinking OpenFlows Architecture product decisions Review of outcomes only agent& 8209;run pipeline OpenFlows reallocates the boring per& 8209;change decisioning back to an automated pipeline - and gives it back to product and architecture. Your chain vs. the OpenFlows chain Without OpenFlows Issue Human reviews each step Code Human reviews PR Human merges + human hours per ticket With OpenFlows Issue Agent plan Agent first& 8209;pass review Agent build + tests Agent adversarial review Agent merge Human at decisions only engineer time freed The trade-offs to weigh OpenFlows requires Coder. It is not a standalone tool; it rides on your self& 8209;hosted Coder environment. If you don't have or don't want that infrastructure, it isn't the right starting point. It favors governance over raw speed. The planning gate and adversarial review add steps. That is the point - they are the source of the audit trail and the quality ceiling - but for trivial, throwaway changes they are more ceremony than you might want. Setup is non& 8209;trivial. Installing it means configuring Manager, PostgreSQL, Redis, Coder, a GitHub OAuth App for sign-in, and a GitHub App for repository access. Humans are moved, not removed. OpenFlows still hands you the architecture and the final decision - you own the product, the direction, and what ships. What it removes is the per& 8209;change accept/deny bottleneck, not the engineer. Where to go next

text: OpenFlows Manager is the trusted product control plane. Coder provides workspace execution. Nexus is the controller inside one tenant's runtime, and workers execute ticket-scoped tasks in separate workspaces. mermaid title="The product control plane provisions and supports a tenant runtime" flowchart TB user "Signed-in user" -- manager "OpenFlows Manager" manager -- postgres PostgreSQL manager -- coder "Coder" manager -- github "GitHub App" coder -- nexus "Nexus controller" coder -- workers "Worker workspaces" nexus redis "Tenant Redis" workers redis Component Boundary Responsibility --- --- --- Manager Product control plane Users, organizations, GitHub connections, runtime identity, broker, operations, hook ingress Coder Execution control plane Templates, builds, workspace agents, and workspace lifecycle Nexus Tenant controller Issue sync, scheduling, reconciliation, agent hooks, and A2A relay Forge, Sentinel, Vessel, Lore Tenant workers Scoped work in separate disposable Coder workspaces PostgreSQL Manager system of record Ownership, operation leases, workspace credentials, and broker leases Redis Tenant coordination store Tickets, worker slots, agent heartbeats, A2A evidence, and hook audit From organization to agent work 1. A user signs into Manager, creates an organization, and connects a GitHub App installation. 2. Manager provisions a tenant and Nexus using durable operations and pinned Coder templates. 3. Nexus registers a runtime session, synchronizes repository work using a brokered installation token, and asks Manager for workers. 4. Manager authorizes and creates workers in Coder. title: The Nexus controller
summary: Nexus is the long-running controller inside a tenant's Coder workspace. It reads repository issues, maintains the ticket flow, assigns roles, detects stalled work, and escalates…
text: Nexus is the long-running controller inside a tenant's Coder workspace. It reads repository issues, maintains the ticket flow, assigns roles, detects stalled work, and escalates decisions requiring a person. Startup Nexus registers with Manager using its workspace bootstrap, opens the tenant-scoped Redis store, starts Manager heartbeats, publishes role-specific agent hooks and assets, and serves the lifecycle hook consumer and A2A JSON-RPC relay. Scheduling Nexus selects a ticket, role, branch, and slot. For hosted workers it calls Manager's runtime workspace API with an idempotency key. Manager checks the caller, capacity, and pinned template, then provisions through Coder. Nexus polls the managed workspace status and adopts it when running. GitHub Nexus asks Manager's broker for a short-lived installation token for API work. It does not need the GitHub App private key or a person's GitHub OAuth token. Reconciliation and recovery The controller repeatedly reads tenant state from Redis and advances the flow. Manager independently reclaims expired provisioning operation leases in PostgreSQL. A failed Nexus pass can be retried; a failed Manager operation has a separate durable status and retry policy. See Manager Runtime /docs/architecture/manager-runtime for the workspace control path and Hooks and A2A /docs/architecture/hooks-and-a2a for its two inbound services.

title: Credentials and trust boundaries
summary: These credentials are separate. A browser session cannot register a workspace; a runtime token cannot access Redis; an A2A token cannot call Manager APIs.
text: These credentials are separate. A browser session cannot register a workspace; a runtime token cannot access Redis; an A2A token cannot call Manager APIs. Credential Bound to Accepted by Where the raw value appears --- --- --- --- Browser session Signed-in user Manager product API Browser cookie Workspace bootstrap One workspace startup Manager registration once Read-only runtime bundle Runtime access and refresh One registered workspace Manager runtime API Workspace process memory Tenant Redis credential One tenant Redis ACL and namespace Mounted bundle / runtime GitHub installation token One authorized repository Git and GitHub API Short-lived workspace process A2A pair token One ticket pair Nexus relay Paired worker parameters Registration and rotation Manager hashes bootstrap, access, and refresh credentials in PostgreSQL. Registration atomically consumes the one-time bootstrap. The runtime uses its access token on Manager calls. When it receives an authorization failure, it rotates the refresh token and retries once. The refresh family has a fixed maximum lifetime. GitHub credential broker mermaid title="Brokered GitHub token exchange" sequenceDiagram participant W as Tenant workspace participant M as Manager broker participant P as PostgreSQL participant G as GitHub App W- M: Runtime token + purpose git or api M- P: Validate workspace, tenant and repository M- G: Sign App request and mint installation token G-- M: Short-lived scoped token M- P: Record encrypted credential lease M-- W: Short-lived token for authorized repository The runtime calls POST /api/v1/runtime/github-credentials with purpose git or api . Manager derives the repository, installation, and permission profile from the authenticated workspace. It signs a GitHub App request using the server-held private key, validates the returned scope, records a lease, and returns a short-lived installation token. Hosted GitHub operations use the App installation identity. A person signs in with GitHub to access OpenFlows and connect the organization; that OAuth login is not the credential Forge uses to push a branch. What a compromised workspace can see A running workspace can read its own bootstrap bundle, tenant Redis credential, current runtime session, and any short-lived GitHub token it has requested. Treat it as a credential-bearing execution environment. It does not receive the Manager master key, GitHub App private key, global Coder operator credential, or another tenant's Redis password. !WARNING Operational boundary Short-lived tokens reduce exposure; they do not make a compromised workspace harmless. Network access, workspace isolation, revocation, audit, and credential rotation remain necessary.

title: Deployment architecture
summary: A production deployment runs Manager as the trusted control plane and Coder as the workspace execution platform. PostgreSQL and Redis serve different kinds of state. GitHub…
text: A production deployment runs Manager as the trusted control plane and Coder as the workspace execution platform. PostgreSQL and Redis serve different kinds of state. GitHub callbacks reach Manager at its public HTTPS origin. Service Role --- --- OpenFlows Manager Product API, authentication, runtime broker, hook ingress, durable provisioning workers PostgreSQL Manager ownership, credentials hashes, operations, workspace and lease state Redis Tenant ACL identities and coordination state Coder and provisioner Workspace builds, agents, template releases, and execution Secret provider Platform keys and per-workspace runtime bundles GitHub OAuth App and GitHub App Human sign-in and repository-scoped installation access Required network paths - Browsers and GitHub reach Manager's HTTPS origin. - Manager reaches PostgreSQL, Redis administration, Coder, GitHub, its secret provider, and each tenant's Nexus hook endpoint. - Coder workspaces reach Manager's runtime API, their tenant Redis endpoint, GitHub, and the Nexus A2A relay when paired. - Coder lifecycle sender reaches Manager's hook ingress, which authenticates and relays events to Nexus. Manager replicas Manager provisioning jobs live in PostgreSQL and are claimed with leases. Another replica can recover a job after a crashed replica's lease expires. Each instance needs the same configuration, secret provider, and access to shared services. Broker request coalescing is currently local to one process. Template releases Template manifests are immutable by release name. Publish a new release when a template changes, promote it for an organization, and update or rebuild workspaces to pick it up. !INFO Operator guide For exact configuration, setup, doctor, and serving commands, use the versioned operator documentation https://github.com/The-AgenticFlow/OpenFlows/tree/main/docs/implementation/centralized-deployment .

title: Decision & Routing
summary: Routing is how work moves between roles. The Controller doesn't command agents with ad-hoc messages; it runs a flow - an ordered map of steps and the allowed transitions between…
text: Routing is how work moves between roles. The Controller doesn't command agents with ad-hoc messages; it runs a flow - an ordered map of steps and the allowed transitions between them - and it is the single place those transitions are declared. This page explains how work is dispatched between roles and how each transition is routed. The routing flow Work moves through the team in a fixed order - NEXUS dispatches, FORGE builds, SENTINEL reviews, VESSEL merges, LORE documents - and then back around to NEXUS: Transition Stage What routes --- --- --- NEXUS → FORGE A ticket’s turn NEXUS assigns a ticket and requests a managed Forge workspace. FORGE → SENTINEL Plan review FORGE finishes a plan and hands it over; SENTINEL reviews and approves before any code is written. FORGE → SENTINEL Review FORGE implements against the approved plan and opens a pull request; SENTINEL reviews it. SENTINEL → VESSEL Merge An approved review routes the pull request to VESSEL to watch CI and merge. VESSEL → LORE Document A successful merge routes the completed work to LORE to document. LORE → NEXUS Loop Documented, merged work returns to NEXUS, which picks up the next ticket. How a step routes to the next Each step follows the same three-part rhythm: 1. Read the current state of the work. 2. Act - do the external work called for provisioning a workspace, writing code, running a review, opening or merging a pull request . 3. Record and route - write the result and hand control to the next allowed step. A transition only happens when the previous step produced the required result - an approved plan, a reviewed pull request, a successful merge. The Controller advances each piece of in-flight work by exactly one step on every beat of its orchestration loop. The declared transitions are the guardrail Because every possible transition is declared in one place, the system can't wander off into an unplanned path. A builder can't route work to a merge on its own, and a reviewer can't begin a build. Each role is only handed the work that the previous step produced: - FORGE can't build without an approved plan. A plan awaiting approval stays with the builder until SENTINEL approves it. - SENTINEL only reviews what's ready - an approved-plan check or a pull-request review - and records a verdict. - VESSEL won't merge an unapproved pull request. Merge is only offered to VESSEL after a review approves it. - LORE only documents merged work. Documentation is triggered by a successful merge. When a path can't continue If an unexpected path is ever taken, the Controller treats it as an anomaly rather than silently ignoring it. And if work can't advance because judgment is needed - an unclear requirement, a security concern, or verification that keeps failing - the work is parked and escalated to a human instead of being routed onward on a guess. The review posture stays strict: when in doubt, don't approve. !INFO Routing is state, not conversation Work is routed by writing results to the shared record of truth, not by sending ad-hoc messages. The Controller re-reads that state on every beat, so a step's result is picked up and handed to the next role automatically - and the routing can be steered live, without restarting.

title: Hooks and agent-to-agent communication
summary: Two hook mechanisms and one A2A relay participate in the runtime. Each has its own sender, authentication, and state.
text: Two hook mechanisms and one A2A relay participate in the runtime. Each has its own sender, authentication, and state. Coder lifecycle events mermaid title="Coder event relay through Manager" sequenceDiagram participant C as Coder participant M as Manager hook ingress participant N as Nexus hook server participant R as Tenant Redis C- M: Signed lifecycle event M- M: Verify signature and tenant mapping M- N: Relay body with tenant signature N- N: Verify tenant signature N- R: Record audit event N-- M: Hook decision M-- C: Hook decision 1. Coder sends a signed lifecycle event to Manager's /api/v1/hooks/coder/chat endpoint. 2. Manager verifies the global signature and payload hash, resolves the Coder workspace to exactly one tenant, then signs the same body with that tenant's hook key. 3. Manager relays the event to the Nexus hook server at /experimental/hooks/chat . Nexus verifies the tenant signature, writes an audit event to tenant Redis, and may wake its flow loop. 4. Nexus returns a hook decision through Manager to the Coder sender. Agent CLI hooks Nexus publishes role-specific shell hooks and agent assets to a shared artifacts volume. A Forge or Sentinel workspace copies its own hooks during startup and configures its local agent client. These local scripts call the harness; they are distinct from Coder's HTTP lifecycle events. Forge and Sentinel A2A verification mermaid title="Forge and Sentinel exchange evidence through Nexus" sequenceDiagram participant S as Sentinel participant N as Nexus A2A relay participant R as Tenant Redis participant F as Forge S- N: Verification task with pair token N- R: Store task and token-bound state F- N: Claim authorized task F- F: Run verification in Forge workspace F- N: Send progress and result N- R: Persist result and audit evidence S- N: Read result N-- S: Verification evidence Nexus derives a ticket pair token and stores its hash in tenant Redis. Manager passes the raw token when it creates the paired worker workspaces. Sentinel sends a verification request to the Nexus JSON-RPC relay. Forge claims the task, runs the allowed verification in its own workspace, and sends progress and results back. Sentinel reads the recorded result without entering Forge's filesystem. The relay stores tasks, results, and audit evidence in tenant Redis so it can recover after a Nexus restart. Manager provisions and scopes the participants, but Forge and Sentinel send A2A traffic directly to Nexus. !INFO Different tokens Coder hook JWTs authenticate lifecycle delivery. A2A pair tokens authenticate one verification pair. Runtime access tokens authenticate workspace calls to Manager. None substitutes for another.

title: How the pieces talk
summary: Manager owns privileged control-plane decisions. Nexus owns the tenant's agent workflow. Coder runs workspaces, and Redis stores tenant coordination state. The channel determines…
text: Manager owns privileged control-plane decisions. Nexus owns the tenant's agent workflow. Coder runs workspaces, and Redis stores tenant coordination state. The channel determines the credential and authority. Channel Authentication What travels over it --- --- --- Nexus → Manager Workspace runtime access token Worker requests, status, heartbeats, and GitHub credential requests Manager → Coder Platform operator credential Template publication and workspace creation or lifecycle Runtime → Redis Tenant Redis ACL credential Ticket state, worker slots, heartbeats, A2A evidence Coder → Manager → Nexus Global then tenant hook JWT Coder lifecycle events and policy responses Forge / Sentinel → Nexus Ticket pair token A2A verification tasks, progress, and results Runtime → GitHub Brokered installation token Repository API and Git operations Runtime API Each workspace registers using a one-time bootstrap and receives an access/refresh pair. Manager derives its tenant, role, and repository from the workspace record. Nexus asks Manager to create workers; Manager records a durable operation and talks to Coder. Hooks and A2A Coder lifecycle events enter through Manager, which authenticates and routes them to the tenant's Nexus hook server. Agent CLI hooks run locally inside worker workspaces. Sentinel and Forge exchange verification tasks through Nexus's A2A relay, which persists evidence to tenant Redis. Read Manager Runtime /docs/architecture/manager-runtime , Credentials and Trust /docs/architecture/credentials , and Hooks and A2A /docs/architecture/hooks-and-a2a for the full request flows.

title: Architecture
summary: This section explains how the OpenFlows system is put together - in plain language, with no code. It's written for anyone who wants to understand the system well enough to operate…
text: This section explains how the OpenFlows system is put together - in plain language, with no code. It's written for anyone who wants to understand the system well enough to operate it, extend it, or evaluate its security. OpenFlows Manager owns product identity, repository connections, runtime authorization, credential brokerage, and durable workspace operations. Coder runs isolated workspaces. A tenant's Nexus controller coordinates agents using tenant-scoped Redis and an A2A relay. Recommended reading order 1. Components and Interactions /docs/architecture/components-and-interactions : identify the independently running parts and trust boundaries. 2. Manager Runtime /docs/architecture/manager-runtime : follow registration and durable provisioning. 3. Credentials and Trust /docs/architecture/credentials : see which token authorizes each connection. 4. Hooks and A2A /docs/architecture/hooks-and-a2a : distinguish lifecycle delivery from tenant-local agent communication. The pages below continue with the controller, worker fleet, recovery, security, and deployment. If you are new to the product, begin with the full documentation reading path /docs . The centre of the picture Nexus requests workers through the Manager runtime API. Manager checks the tenant, role, quota, and pinned template, records a durable operation, and calls Coder to create the workspace. Forge, Sentinel, Vessel, and Lore run inside those workspaces. Nexus never needs the platform Coder operator credential. The architecture is built on a simple thesis: architecture is the product . OpenFlows encodes the engineering - the review gates, the recovery patterns, the trusted boundaries - so that agents produce software, not just code. The guardrails that run through the whole design are straightforward: plan before code , when in doubt, don't approve , and bounded recovery then human escalation . Workspaces receive scoped runtime and Redis credentials; platform signing keys remain in Manager. !INFO The flow in brief A GitHub issue is turned into a ticket \\u2192 dispatched to FORGE to plan and build \\u2192 reviewed at a distance by SENTINEL \\u2192 merged by VESSEL once CI is green \\u2192 documented by LORE \\u2192 the workspace is torn down. Every step is an approved transition, and the whole cycle is self-healing and auditable. cards - Big Picture /docs/architecture/big-picture : The control plane and the work plane, and how the two halves fit together. - Components and Interactions /docs/architecture/components-and-interactions : The component boundaries and the authenticated paths between them. - Manager Runtime /docs/architecture/manager-runtime : How workspaces register, request workers, and recover through Manager. - Credentials and Trust /docs/architecture/credentials : Runtime sessions, repository tokens, Redis access, and trust boundaries. - Hooks and A2A /docs/architecture/hooks-and-a2a : Coder lifecycle ingress, agent hooks, and Forge–Sentinel verification. - The Controller /docs/architecture/controller : The long-lived “brain” that ingests work, dispatches agents, and keeps the team moving. - The Workspace Fleet /docs/architecture/workspace-fleet : One long-lived orchestrator workspace and many short-lived, disposable worker workspaces — and how they stay isolated. - How the Pieces Talk /docs/architecture/how-the-pieces-talk : The three channels that keep the team in sync — and the difference between facts and live tasks. - State Machine & Recovery /docs/architecture/state-machine-recovery : The steady “read everything, nudge everything, repeat” beat that makes the system self-healing. - Decision & Routing /docs/architecture/decision-routing : How work is dispatched between roles and how transitions are declared and routed through the pipeline. - Security by Design /docs/architecture/security-by-design : Trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, isolation, and limitations. - How It’s Deployed /docs/architecture/deployment : The reference deployment: the five pieces, how they’re grouped, and standing it up for many teams.

title: The Manager-mediated runtime
summary: OpenFlows Manager is the authority for users, organizations, GitHub connections, tenants, workspace records, and runtime permissions. Coder builds and runs workspaces; Nexus…
text: OpenFlows Manager is the authority for users, organizations, GitHub connections, tenants, workspace records, and runtime permissions. Coder builds and runs workspaces; Nexus coordinates work within one tenant. How a workspace starts mermaid title="Workspace registration and runtime session" sequenceDiagram participant M as Manager participant C as Coder participant W as Workspace participant P as PostgreSQL M- P: Record workspace and one-time bootstrap hash M- C: Create workspace from pinned template C- W: Start with scoped runtime bundle W- M: POST /api/v1/runtime/register M- P: Consume bootstrap and store token hashes M-- W: Access token and rotating refresh token loop While running W- M: Authenticated heartbeat M- P: Check workspace and tenant state end 1. Manager records a workspace and prepares a read-only runtime bundle with its workspace ID, tenant ID, Manager URL, one-time bootstrap, Redis access, and tenant hook key. 2. Manager's operation worker asks Coder to create the workspace using a pinned template release. 3. The workspace submits its bootstrap to POST /api/v1/runtime/register . Manager consumes it once and returns a short-lived access token and rotating refresh token. 4. The process sends heartbeats to Manager. Manager checks its workspace, tenant, organization, connection, and credential state on privileged requests. How Nexus starts workers mermaid title="Durable worker provisioning" sequenceDiagram participant N as Nexus participant M as Manager API participant P as PostgreSQL participant Q as Manager worker participant C as Coder N- M: Request worker with idempotency key M- P: Authorize, reserve slot, enqueue operation M-- N: Operation ID Q- P: Claim leased operation Q- C: Create scoped worker workspace C-- Q: Workspace state Q- P: Record result N- M: Poll operation and adopt worker Nexus chooses the role, ticket, branch, and slot, then requests a worker through POST /api/v1/runtime/workspaces with an idempotency key. Manager verifies that the caller is this tenant's Nexus, reserves capacity, and writes a durable operation. A Manager worker claims the operation and asks Coder to create the Forge, Sentinel, Vessel, or Lore workspace. Nexus polls the workspace status and adopts the worker once it is running. Database leases let a different Manager instance reclaim provisioning work after a process crash. Repeating the same request does not create a second worker. Where state lives - PostgreSQL: resource ownership, operations, runtime credential hashes, generations, and GitHub credential leases. - Redis: tenant coordination, agent heartbeats, worker slots, hook audit, and A2A task evidence, protected by tenant credentials and namespace. - Coder: workspace, build, and agent execution state. - Secret provider: platform keys, bootstrap values, tenant credentials, and mounted runtime bundles. !INFO Two control loops Manager supervises durable workspace operations and runtime registration. Nexus supervises the tenant's issue-to-PR workflow and agent progress. cards - Credentials and Trust /docs/architecture/credentials : What each token authorizes and where it lives. - Hooks and A2A /docs/architecture/hooks-and-a2a : How events and agent messages cross workspaces.

title: State Machine & Recovery
summary: The heart of the Controller is a simple, intentionally boring loop that acts as the system's state machine. Understanding it is understanding how OpenFlows stays correct and…
text: The heart of the Controller is a simple, intentionally boring loop that acts as the system's state machine. Understanding it is understanding how OpenFlows stays correct and self-healing over long, messy runs. The loop in one line Every few seconds: re-read the whole system, advance every piece of work one step, repair what's broken, repeat. Why "read everything, every time" The Controller deliberately keeps almost no state of its own. On each beat it re-reads the entire system from the coordination store - all tickets, all workers, all pull requests, all heartbeats - and figures out fresh what needs to happen. This is not wasteful; it's the source of the system's correctness: - It converges. Even if a step failed halfway through the last beat, this beat sees the true state and sets it right. - It self-heals. A workspace that went silent, a chat that errored, a pull request nobody merged - the loop rediscovers each and fixes it. - It restarts cleanly. Nothing important depends on the Controller's memory surviving, because the memory lives in the store. What one beat does A single beat walks the whole team end to end and lets each role advance its affairs by one step: 1. NEXUS syncs GitHub issues and pull requests, reconciles the fleet, repairs broken pieces, and dispatches any ticket whose turn it is. 2. FORGE advances any in-flight build - handling a plan awaiting approval, a build in progress, or a pull request just opened. 3. SENTINEL reviews anything that's ready - an approved-plan check or a pull-request review - and records a verdict. 4. VESSEL watches pending pull requests through CI and merges the green ones. 5. LORE documents anything that just merged. Most beats, most things are idle or mid-flight, and the beat is cheap. The loop only does work when there's work to do. "A bad beat must never kill the brain" The most important safety rule in the loop: !WARNING Log it and move on If one beat errors, log it and move on. Never let a bad beat take down the Controller. A one-off failure - a slow API, a hiccup on the network, a workspace that failed to come up - is absorbed and forgotten by the next beat. A persistent fault is retried every beat until it clears. The bounded-retry-and-escalate rule Recovery is powerful but not infinite. The loop repairs broken work up to a bounded number of attempts . If a ticket keeps failing past that limit, the loop stops retrying, parks the ticket, and escalates it to a human - with a notification and links. It chooses "ask for help" over "spin forever." Roughly speaking, recoverable failures are infrastructure problems - a stopped workspace, a pull request not yet merged, a misbehaving response that can be retried. Human-escalated failures are judgment problems - an unclear requirement, work that contradicts the plan, or a security concern that needs a person's call. Steering the loop live Because the loop re-reads state every beat, you can steer it without restarting : - Pause - let in-flight work finish but don't pick up anything new. - Drain - stop taking new tickets. - Target - focus only on a specific repository, issue, or label. - Resume / normal - back to business as usual. These are stored as state, read every beat, and applied on the very next pass. Live steering with zero downtime. The takeaway OpenFlows doesn't try to be perfect in any single moment. It is built to keep trying - to read reality, nudge it forward, absorb failures, and converge - which is exactly the behavior you want in an autonomous system running around the clock.

title: Security model
summary: OpenFlows separates platform authority from tenant execution. Manager holds infrastructure signing and provisioning credentials; Coder runs the workspaces; Nexus coordinates a…
text: OpenFlows separates platform authority from tenant execution. Manager holds infrastructure signing and provisioning credentials; Coder runs the workspaces; Nexus coordinates a tenant's agents. Every runtime API call resolves scope from a registered workspace. Controls and boundaries Boundary Enforcement --- --- Platform secrets GitHub App signing key, Coder operator credential, and Manager encryption key remain in the trusted control plane. Runtime identity One-time workspace bootstrap, hashed access and refresh credentials, and server-derived scope. GitHub access Brokered installation token limited to the authorized repository and role-specific permissions. Tenant coordination Tenant Redis ACL credential plus immutable tenant namespace. Provisioning Durable operations, database leases, capacity reservations, and idempotent requests. Coder lifecycle ingress Manager verifies a global JWT, resolves the workspace to a tenant, and re-signs the event for Nexus. A2A verification Ticket pair token, Forge-only claim, tenant-scoped task and audit records. Workspace exposure A worker is isolated and disposable, but it is not credential-free. Its mounted bundle contains a one-time bootstrap and tenant Redis access. It holds a runtime session and may receive short-lived GitHub installation tokens for its repository. A compromised workspace can act within those scopes until the credentials expire or are revoked. Manager does not mount its database connection, GitHub App private key, Coder operator token, or master encryption key into workspaces. Repository permissions are selected on the server, and the runtime cannot name a different installation or permission set in its request. Independent review Forge and Sentinel have separate workspaces. Sentinel asks Forge to run verification through Nexus's A2A relay, receives recorded evidence, and does not enter Forge's filesystem. Missing or invalid evidence must not approve a review gate. Operational responsibilities Operators must secure network paths, the secret provider, PostgreSQL, Redis, Coder, template releases, logs, and backup copies. The current GitHub broker coalesces equivalent requests within a Manager process; distributed single-flight across replicas remains an improvement. !INFO Inspect the protocols See Credentials and Trust /docs/architecture/credentials for token lifecycles and Hooks and A2A /docs/architecture/hooks-and-a2a for event authentication.

title: The workspace fleet
summary: Each tenant has a Nexus controller workspace and may have Forge, Sentinel, Vessel, and Lore worker workspaces. Manager records their owner, role, tenant, desired state, Coder…
text: Each tenant has a Nexus controller workspace and may have Forge, Sentinel, Vessel, and Lore worker workspaces. Manager records their owner, role, tenant, desired state, Coder identity, and pinned template release. Coder builds and runs them. Nexus Nexus is long-running. It coordinates tickets and hosts the A2A relay and tenant lifecycle hook server. It calls Manager to request or supervise workers, and it accesses its repository through the GitHub credential broker. Workers Workers are role-scoped and can be removed after their assignment. They have separate filesystems and use a ticket pair token when participating in A2A verification. Their startup uses a mounted runtime bundle and a brokered, short-lived GitHub installation token for repository access. Credential boundary A workspace can read its own tenant Redis credential, runtime session, and temporary GitHub token. It cannot read Manager's GitHub App private key, Coder operator token, or another tenant's Redis credential. Do not treat a running agent workspace as a credential-free sandbox. Liveness and cleanup Workspaces heartbeat to Manager, while agent progress and assignment heartbeats live in tenant Redis. Manager records lifecycle state durably. Nexus uses the coordination signals to detect stale agents and request recovery. Cleanup revokes runtime authority and releases capacity. !INFO Separate controls Manager controls workspace identity and lifecycle. Nexus controls the tenant's workflow. Coder reports build and agent execution state.

title: The Agent Registry
summary: The agent registry is how you configure your team. Who is on it, how many of them, what model they use, and which skills and tools they have - all of it lives here, and you can…
text: The agent registry is how you configure your team. Who is on it, how many of them, what model they use, and which skills and tools they have - all of it lives here, and you can change it without a restart or redeploy. What the registry controls For each role on the team, the registry defines: Setting What it controls --- --- How many workers The concurrency ceiling for each role - how many instances may run at once. Which model The model each agent uses. Whether approval is required Whether the agent must get approval before acting plan mode . Which skills The skills available to the agent. Which tools The tools and servers it can call. Where it lives The registry is kept in the control plane , inside the coordination store - not in a file you edit and redeploy. It is the single source of truth for the team's configuration. How you change it You edit the registry through the control panel . The change is validated, and then it takes effect on the team's next cycle. No restart, no redeploy, no waiting for a maintenance window. Change a role's model or add a skill, and the running team picks it up almost immediately. The safety rule: you can't accidentally zero out a role Changing configurations can be risky if done blindly. The registry enforces a guardrail: an override can never silently drive a role down to zero workers. If a change would leave a role with no capacity, it is rejected rather than applied, so you can't accidentally disable your whole builder fleet with a bad edit. Adding skills, tools, and models The common way to extend the team is through the registry, with configuration-only changes: Extension How it works --- --- Add a skill A skill definition is added and referenced on a role. Add a tool or server Register it on the role, or centrally. Both can work together. Enable a model Configure it and reference it on the role. These are configuration-only changes. Building a brand-new role with its own persona, workspace template, and routing is the one change that touches the system's internals - a deliberate, less-common action. !INFO The panel and the command surface never drift The web control panel is the everyday home of the registry. From it you see the live team - roles, their sizes, their models - and edit the fleet directly. It rides on the same state and commands as the command-line surface, so the two can never drift out of sync.

title: The Agent Team
summary: OpenFlows runs a group of AI agents that cooperate like a real engineering team. Each agent has one primary job, and together they close the loop from issue to merged pull…
text: OpenFlows runs a group of AI agents that cooperate like a real engineering team. Each agent has one primary job, and together they close the loop from issue to merged pull request. The team has five roles. The five roles Agent Role What it does Reviews before acting? --- --- --- --- NEXUS Orchestrator Owns the whole pipeline: picks up issues, assigns work, coordinates the team, recovers from failures, and notifies humans when needed. Yes FORGE Builder Writes code against an agreed plan, creates branches, and opens pull requests. No SENTINEL Reviewer Adversarially reviews plans and code for security, quality, and test coverage. Yes VESSEL DevOps Watches CI, resolves merge conflicts, and merges green pull requests. No LORE Writer Documents decisions and updates changelogs after a merge. Often disabled by default. No What "reviews before acting" means The roles that review and gate - the orchestrator and the reviewer - are designed to check before they proceed rather than blindly move ahead. The builder, DevOps, and writer roles act directly, but their actions are bounded by gates: the builder can't build without an approved plan, DevOps won't merge an unapproved pull request, and the writer only documents merged work. How they act like a team The team is sequential where it must be and parallel where it can be . Each transition only happens when the previous step produced the required result - an approved plan, a reviewed pull request, a successful merge. Hand-off What happens --- --- NEXUS plans the assignment Hands work to an idle builder. FORGE writes and stops Waits until its plan is approved. SENTINEL reviews Never touches the builder’s workspace. VESSEL merges And tears down the workspace. LORE documents Records the completed work. Roles are configured, not hard-coded Which roles exist, how many workers each role can run at once, what model each uses, and what skills and tools are available - all of this is kept in the agent registry , which lives in the control plane and can be changed without a restart or redeploy. What an agent workspace looks like Each agent runs in its own isolated, disposable workspace: - No LLM API keys. - No raw repository credentials. - Heavily restricted network access the control plane, GitHub, and the coordination store - and little else . The agent coordinates with the team strictly through a small, typed command surface - it never talks directly to the coordination store. This is what keeps the whole system safe and auditable. Adding to the team You can extend what the team can do without writing code by adding skills, tools, or models through the registry. Adding a brand-new role is the one extension that touches the system's internals. !INFO Review is a separate role, not a prompt The reviewer is not a prompt attached to the builder. It is a separate agent with a separate workspace and a separate model, which is exactly what makes adversarial review meaningful. A writer and a reviewer never share a filesystem.

title: The Coder / OpenFlows split
summary: Coder decides where agents execute. Manager decides which user and tenant may run a workspace, which template and repository it uses, and what scoped credentials it may receive.…
text: Coder decides where agents execute. Manager decides which user and tenant may run a workspace, which template and repository it uses, and what scoped credentials it may receive. Nexus decides how agents collaborate on that tenant's work. Component Primary responsibility --- --- Coder Build and execute isolated workspaces; report build and agent state OpenFlows Manager Authorize users and runtimes; broker GitHub credentials; provision workspaces through Coder Nexus Coordinate one tenant's issue-to-PR flow, worker assignments, hooks, and A2A evidence The Manager holds the platform Coder operator credential and GitHub App private key. Nexus and workers register as workspace runtimes and receive only their own tenant-scoped bundle and short-lived credentials. Manager asks Coder to perform workspace lifecycle operations on their behalf. Read Manager Runtime /docs/architecture/manager-runtime and Credentials and Trust /docs/architecture/credentials for the protocol and security boundaries.

title: Architecture-First Development
summary: OpenFlows is built on a simple thesis: architecture is the product. The system does not just generate code - it encodes the engineering discipline that separates production…
text: OpenFlows is built on a simple thesis: architecture is the product. The system does not just generate code - it encodes the engineering discipline that separates production software from a pile of confident, well-written changes. This page explains what that discipline is and why it is structural. Code is cheap. Thinking is not. Writing code against a specification has become cheap. What stays hard is thinking : understanding the architecture, making product judgments, and keeping security and quality in mind. A team of agents that simply write code would produce impressive-looking work that solves the wrong problem, drifts from your conventions, and skips the careful review gates you rely on. OpenFlows encodes that discipline as an automated team. It turns the judgment steps - planning, review, verification, and recovery - into enforced parts of the pipeline, applied to every issue, consistently, rather than left to chance. Putting each actor at the right level of the chain The insight behind OpenFlows is that software teams already have the right people - they are often just operating at the wrong level. A person should own the architecture and the product : what to build, why it matters, and how it should hold together. They should not be the bottleneck that reads every line an agent produces. Because agents write faster than people can review, the first-pass review of agent-written code has to come from another agent - that is what makes the pipeline scale at all. - Agents write, test, review as a first pass , merge, and document - the repetitive, low-judgment work, run in a well-defined pipeline. - Humans own the architecture and product decisions - the security calls, the ambiguous requirements, the direction - and are pulled in only at those boundaries instead of clicking accept or deny all day. This is not about replacing engineers. It is about moving them to the level of the chain where they create the most value. The guardrails that make it "engineering," not just coding Four principles run through the whole design, and each is enforced by the system rather than suggested to the agents: - Plan before code. No agent starts writing until a plan is agreed. This is the planning gate /docs/concepts/planning-gate . - When in doubt, don't approve. The reviewer blocks rather than guesses when evidence is missing - it would rather hold a ticket or escalate than merge something unverified. - Bounded recovery, then human escalation. The system repairs what it can, a bounded number of times, then asks a person rather than spinning forever. - No secrets in worker workspaces. Trust, keys, and credentials stay concentrated in the control plane; the work plane is disposable and keyless. See Security by Design /docs/architecture/security-by-design . Why it is structural, not a suggestion These guardrails are not prompts an agent could ignore. The planning gate cannot be skipped, approvals are single-use, the reviewer works in an isolated workspace, and recovery is bounded. Because the discipline is structural, you can leave the team running and trust that it will not cut corners - which is exactly what makes autonomy safe. What this buys you - Consistent judgment. The same plan, review, and verification discipline is applied to every issue. - Trustworthy autonomy. The system can be left to run because it won't bypass the engineering steps. - An audit trail. Every plan approval and review verdict is a recorded, attributable event. !INFO Architecture as the product The value of OpenFlows is not that the agents write code - any assistant can do that. It is that the architecture, contracts, and review gates produce software , not just code. Where to go next cards - The Planning Gate /docs/concepts/planning-gate : The structural rule that starts every ticket. - The Agent Team /docs/concepts/agent-team : The roles that carry out the disciplined pipeline. - The Controller /docs/architecture/controller : The brain that runs the orchestration loop.

title: The Coordination Store
summary: Every agent, every ticket, every approval, every review, and every pull request is tracked in one place: the coordination store. It is the single record of truth that makes the…
text: Every agent, every ticket, every approval, every review, and every pull request is tracked in one place: the coordination store. It is the single record of truth that makes the team behave like a coherent organisation rather than a set of disconnected systems. OpenFlows is a distributed system - many workspaces, many agents, all working at once. If each of those workspaces kept its own copy of what was happening, they would drift apart and start to contradict one another. By routing everything through a single store, OpenFlows guarantees that the whole team sees the same state and that no step can be skipped or forged. What the store holds The coordination store is the shared, durable memory of the team. It records everything the team needs to agree on to stay consistent. What it tracks Why it matters --- --- Tickets Every piece of work OpenFlows knows about, and the current state of each one. Worker slots Which agent is available, busy, or assigned to a ticket. Pull requests The pull requests awaiting a merge. Phases and history Each ticket’s current phase and the trail that led there. Approvals The single-use approvals that unlock gated steps. Reviews Review verdicts and their outcomes. Liveness The signal that a workspace is still alive and working. Team configuration The live agent registry and the pause and resume control state. Who is allowed to write This is a strict design rule: exactly two things may ever write to the coordination store. - The orchestrator , the central brain, which writes planning, assignment, and fleet state. - The worker command surface , the only way an agent inside a workspace records its phase, approvals, reviews, and heartbeats. Everything else - and in particular the agents themselves - cannot touch it. Writes are validated, so malformed or out-of-order writes are rejected rather than silently accepted. This is what makes "the store is the source of truth" a real guarantee rather than a hope. !INFO The store is a source of truth, not a place to poke around Most operators interact with the store through the control panel, which surfaces current tickets, worker status, pending pull requests, and escalations. Day to day you rarely interact with the store directly - the panel sits on top of it, and the store underneath keeps everything consistent. Durable by design The store is configured for durable storage, so the team's record survives restarts. This is what allows OpenFlows to pause mid-flight, restart, and pick up exactly where it left off. The team does not forget where it was just because a process stopped.

title: Human Escalation
summary: OpenFlows is autonomous, but it is deliberately not unsupervised. There are decisions that should always be made by a person, and the system is engineered to hand those to you…
text: OpenFlows is autonomous, but it is deliberately not unsupervised. There are decisions that should always be made by a person, and the system is engineered to hand those to you clearly and reliably. Escalation is a feature, not a failure: it is a controlled stop rather than a crash. When OpenFlows pulls a human in A ticket escalates to a human when it genuinely needs a judgment call: Reason What it looks like --- --- A security decision Something touches a security boundary and only a person should judge it. An ambiguous or underspecified requirement The work is unclear and the team must not guess. An architectural choice A design direction that needs a human call. A merge block or conflict A merge conflict or block the team cannot resolve on its own. It also escalates after exhausted automatic recovery : if the system has retried a failing ticket a bounded number of times and it is still stuck, it stops retrying and tells you rather than spinning forever. What happens on escalation 1. The ticket is parked - set aside so it doesn't deadlock the rest of the fleet. 2. The worker is released back to the pool. 3. You get a notification on your configured channels with the ticket, the reason, and direct links to the workspace and the pull request. Notifications are carefully rate-limited so you never get flooded. If a channel is down, that never breaks the system itself - it just means you check the panel. How you resolve an escalation You can How the team responds --- --- Comment on or close the GitHub issue The team reacts on its next cycle, reopening or closing the ticket as appropriate. Answer directly in the workspace or chat Give the agent guidance and it resumes with your direction. Reset the work Start clean by resetting the stuck work back to the start and letting the team take another pass. Why the system can't just approve around you OpenFlows' whole posture is "when in doubt, don't approve." The gates are structural, so there is no way for an agent to bypass a review or approve without evidence. An unresolved escalation is a dead end until a person or a legitimate reset intervenes. !TIP You are in the loop where your judgment adds value You are in the loop exactly where your judgment adds value - on the decisions - and out of the loop everywhere a well-guarded team can proceed on its own.

title: Core Concepts
summary: OpenFlows runs a disciplined engineering team of AI agents that coordinate through a shared, governed system. The concepts in this section are the vocabulary the rest of the…
text: OpenFlows runs a disciplined engineering team of AI agents that coordinate through a shared, governed system. The concepts in this section are the vocabulary the rest of the documentation uses: who the team is, how a ticket travels from issue to merged pull request, why the team plans before it codes, where the coordination state lives, where work actually runs, and how security holds together. If you are deciding whether OpenFlows fits your organisation, read these pages first. If you are already running it, they explain the reasoning behind the behaviour you see in production. !INFO One idea anchors everything Coder governs where agents run. OpenFlows governs how they coordinate. This founding split explains the architecture, and the other concepts build on it. Concepts at a Glance Concept What problem it solves Read more --- --- --- The Team Five specialised agents with narrow roles and enforced hand-offs, so no single agent both writes and reviews its own work. Details → /docs/concepts/agent-team The Ticket Lifecycle A fixed path from GitHub issue to merged pull request, with recovery and human escalation as part of the loop. Details → /docs/getting-started/lifecycle-steps The Planning Gate No code before an approved plan; the gate is structural and single-use approvals can’t be replayed. Details → /docs/concepts/planning-gate The Coordination Store A shared, durable record of truth that only the orchestrator and the worker command surface may write. Details → /docs/concepts/coordination-store Workspaces Isolated execution seats with workspace-scoped credentials and a recorded identity. Details → /docs/concepts/workspaces Tenants Strictly separated teams on one server, isolated by both identity and namespaced coordination state. Details → /docs/concepts/tenants Human Escalation The system stops and hands you the decisions that need a judgment call, rather than guessing. Details → /docs/concepts/human-escalation The Agent Registry Team configuration without code or restarts, with a guardrail against accidentally zeroing a role. Details → /docs/concepts/agent-registry The Coder / OpenFlows Split Coder governs where agents run; OpenFlows governs how they coordinate. The founding asymmetry. Details → /docs/concepts/coder-openflows-split How the Concepts Fit Together OpenFlows is an orchestration layer that turns a self-hosted runtime into an autonomous engineering team. The Coder / OpenFlows split sets the stage: the runtime provides governed, ephemeral workspaces and real identity, while OpenFlows supplies the coordination that makes them a team. The agent team plans, builds, reviews, merges, and documents, and each ticket moves through a fixed lifecycle . The planning gate keeps every ticket honest by refusing to advance work without an approved plan. All of this is held together by the coordination store - the single source of truth - and configured through the agent registry . Tenants isolate many teams on one server, and human escalation keeps a person in the loop exactly where a judgment call is needed. Where to Start cards - Architecture-First /docs/concepts/architecture-first : Why OpenFlows plans before it codes, how the planning gate works, and the "when in doubt, don’t approve" rule. - The Agent Team /docs/concepts/agent-team : NEXUS, FORGE, SENTINEL, VESSEL, and LORE — their roles, how they work in sequence and in parallel, and how they’re configured. - The Ticket Lifecycle /docs/getting-started/lifecycle-steps : How an issue becomes a merged pull request, the fixed phases, and what happens when work gets stuck. - The Planning Gate /docs/concepts/planning-gate : Plan before code: why it’s structural, how the gate is enforced, and why the system blocks rather than guesses. - The Coordination Store /docs/concepts/coordination-store : The single record of truth that keeps every agent, ticket, approval, and review consistent. - Workspaces /docs/concepts/workspaces : Where work actually runs: thin, isolated, disposable workspaces with real identity and tight networks. - Tenants /docs/concepts/tenants : How one server serves many teams — what a tenant is, how isolation is enforced, and how you manage one. - Human Escalation /docs/concepts/human-escalation : When a human gets pulled in, what happens on escalation, and the three ways you can resolve it. - The Agent Registry /docs/concepts/agent-registry : How the team is configured without code — roles, models, skills, and tools — and the zero-capacity safety rule. - The Coder / OpenFlows Split /docs/concepts/coder-openflows-split : The founding idea: Coder governs where agents run; OpenFlows governs how they coordinate. !TIP Read the split first, then the gate If you're new, start with the Coder / OpenFlows split to get the mental model, then the planning gate to see how discipline is enforced. The rest of the concepts fill in the details.

title: The Planning Gate
summary: The planning gate is one of the most important ideas in OpenFlows, because it is what turns "an AI that writes code" into "an AI that works like a disciplined engineer."
text: The planning gate is one of the most important ideas in OpenFlows, because it is what turns "an AI that writes code" into "an AI that works like a disciplined engineer." The problem it solves Given a spec, code is cheap. The hard, valuable work is deciding what to build before writing it. If you let an agent start typing immediately, you often end up with confident, well-written code that solves the wrong problem. The planning gate forces the team to agree on the plan first. How it works 1. The builder takes the ticket and produces a written plan describing how it intends to implement it. 2. The builder stops . Even though it is fully capable of writing code, it waits. 3. The reviewer reviews the plan - the same adversarial reviewer that later reviews the code. 4. Only an approved plan unlocks the build phase. Why the system can enforce it This is not a convention or a prompt that an agent could ignore. The planning gate is structural : - A ticket can only enter the pipeline through the planning phase. - Moving out of planning requires consuming an approval that only the reviewer role can create. - That approval is single-use - it can be consumed once, and a second attempt finds nothing. An agent physically cannot skip the review, approve its own plan, or replay a stale approval. If you look at a ticket and it has no approval, there is no path forward for it. "Let's just skip the review" is not possible, even by accident. What this buys you - No code before a plan. You never get an agent barreling ahead on a misunderstanding. - A reviewable decision. The plan and its approval are part of the recorded history. - Trustworthy autonomy. The system can be left to run because it won't cut this corner. The "when in doubt, don't approve" principle The reviewer's job is to be strict. If it cannot verify the required evidence - a plan it can read, a change it can review, a test result that was actually recorded - it must not approve. The system would rather hold a ticket, or escalate it to a human, than merge something unverified. This bias toward "block rather than guess" runs through the whole product. !INFO Plan before code Planning first is the cheapest correctness strategy available. A rejected plan costs little; a confident implementation of the wrong thing costs a great deal more. The planning gate keeps the team aligned before a single line is written. Where to go next cards - Architecture-First Development /docs/concepts/architecture-first : Why planning, review, and structure are the whole product. - Lifecycle Steps /docs/getting-started/lifecycle-steps : See the gate in its place in the ticket lifecycle. - Security by Design /docs/architecture/security-by-design : How single-use approvals protect the gate.

title: Tenants
summary: OpenFlows Manager serves multiple organizations and tenants. A tenant is one repository automation environment within an organization.
text: OpenFlows Manager serves multiple organizations and tenants. A tenant is one repository automation environment within an organization. If you only have one team, you still have "a tenant" - you just have one. Think of a tenant as "one project and one repository." What a tenant is A tenant binds these records and resources: - An OpenFlows organization and its creator-owned Coder workspace identity. - A repository binding - the GitHub repository that team works on. - An orchestrator workspace that runs that team's pipeline. How isolation is enforced Tenants are isolated in two independent ways at the same time: 1. Runtime identity. Manager derives tenant and repository scope from each authenticated workspace. 2. Coordination state. Each tenant has a Redis ACL credential and immutable namespace. The Manager and Redis checks reinforce one another. Operators must still protect the shared services, secrets, and network paths. What this means in practice - Many teams, one server. Run several independent OpenFlows teams sharing the same control plane and coordination store. - No cross-talk. One team's tickets, workers, and pull requests are invisible to another. - Simple operations. Administrators manage tenants from the control panel - add a team, list teams, clean up a stuck team, or remove one entirely. Managing a tenant From the control panel, an operator can manage the tenants currently running: Action What it does --- --- Add Create a tenant for a repository so its team can start working. List See the tenants currently running. Clean Reset a stuck tenant - clear stale or failed work back to the start so the team can take another pass. Remove Take down a tenant and its fleet entirely. Cleanup is an important operational tool. If a tenant's work is wedged and automated recovery has already given up, resetting it back to a clean state is the way to get the loop moving again.

title: Contributing Skills Content
summary: Skills are the configuration-only way to teach a role something new - a workflow, a project convention, a linting process. Because a skill is packaged instructions rather than…
text: Skills are the configuration-only way to teach a role something new - a workflow, a project convention, a linting process. Because a skill is packaged instructions rather than system code, contributing good skill content is one of the lightest and most accessible ways to help the project. How skills work A skill is a set of instructions a role can load on demand. It typically captures a repeatable capability - how this project runs its checks, the conventions we follow for this kind of work, the steps for that process - and it is scoped per role, so the builder and the reviewer can carry different skills. Each skill is configured into a role through the team configuration, without any system code change. For the full walkthrough of what a skill is and how a role picks one up, see the Adding a Skill /docs/guides/extending-skills guide. Contributing skills content From a contributor’s perspective, a skill contribution is a documentation-and-content change: - Describe the capability clearly. State what outcome the skill produces, when a role should use it, and what inputs and outputs it needs. - Write precise instructions. A good skill is specific enough to be followed deterministically and includes a worked example. - Document failure modes. What can go wrong, how to detect it, and what the role should do next. - Keep it scoped. One skill does one thing. If a contribution needs to change how the system itself behaves, it’s a core feature, not a skill. !INFO No code change required Adding skill content should never require touching system code. If your proposal needs that, it isn’t a skill - it belongs in a core-feature discussion instead. Align on the approach before investing in the content. How a skill contribution enters the project A skills-content contribution follows the same review-before-merge path as any other change: check existing work to avoid duplication, make a focused change, keep quality high, and open a pull request that explains what you added and why. Maintainers review it with the project’s standards in mind before merging. Related - Adding a Skill /docs/guides/extending-skills - how skills work and how a role uses one. - Contributor Guide /docs/contributing - the contribution workflow.

title: Development Setup
summary: This page describes what you need to set up a local development environment for the OpenFlows project. It is written for contributors who want to build, run, or extend the work,…
text: This page describes what you need to set up a local development environment for the OpenFlows project. It is written for contributors who want to build, run, or extend the work, in plain language and without commands. What the project needs OpenFlows is an open project, and its documentation website is part of the same repository. To develop locally you need a working Node.js toolchain, then you install the project's dependencies. The project's build tooling Astro, for the website is declared in the repository, so a fresh clone plus an install yields a working local environment. The core workflow Once dependencies are installed, the standard loop is straightforward: - Run it locally with live reload while you work - edits show up immediately. - Build a production output to verify the site compiles cleanly from scratch. - Preview the built output before pushing, so what you ship is what you verified. For detailed, copy-paste commands, refer to the project's README in the repository root. It documents the exact steps to install dependencies, start the local server, and build for production. Where to find things in the repository - Website source - the user-facing site you are reading layouts, pages, and components lives under the src tree. - Documentation content - the source Markdown behind these pages lives in the website-docs directory. - Project configuration - the site configuration and its dependencies are declared at the repository root. Governance at a glance OpenFlows' own organizing idea - plan before you build, review before you merge - extends to how the project itself operates: - Small, focused changes move quickly: open, review, merge. - Non-trivial features are discussed and aligned on before implementation, so the approach is agreed before code is written - mirroring the planning gate. - Security-sensitive work gets extra care, consistent with the product's "when in doubt, don't approve" posture. OpenFlows is versioned and released in a controlled way: releases bundle a single, coherent version of the system, and are handled through the project's release tooling and workflows. The documentation website ships with the project and is published automatically from its main branch, so the docs you see are tied to the current state of the codebase. Roles in the project - Maintainers review and merge contributions and steward the architecture. - Contributors that's you propose and build improvements. - Users surface issues and feature ideas that drive direction. !TIP Align early For anything non-trivial, align early - a short discussion before writing code saves a rejected pull request. The project's review culture is rigorous by design; that is what keeps the project and the product trustworthy. Where to go next cards - Contributor Guide /docs/contributing : The full path from idea to merged change. - Testing /docs/contributing/testing : How changes are verified before merging. - Adding Skills /docs/contributing/adding-skills : Contribute capability content, configuration only.

title: Editing the website and docs
summary: How to change blog posts, docs pages and the FAQ from the content editor at openflows.dev/admin, without touching code.
text: How to change blog posts, docs pages and the FAQ from the content editor at openflows.dev/admin, without touching code. !TIP Nothing goes live by accident Every change you make in the editor becomes a draft first. It is only published after it is marked Ready and merged, so you can save as often as you like. 1. Sign in Open openflows.dev/admin https://openflows.dev/admin and choose Sign In with GitHub . You need write access to the openflows-website repository on GitHub. If the button does not work for you, ask a maintainer to add you. 2. Find what you want to change The left column lists everything you can edit: In the editor What it is Where it appears --- --- --- Blog posts Articles /blog Research papers Papers and technical reports /research Case studies Stories from teams using OpenFlows /resources Introduction … Resources One entry per section of the docs /docs, in the sidebar Site content → FAQ The questions and answers /faq and the homepage Authors People credited on blog posts Blog bylines Click a section to see its pages in a table. Click a column title to sort by it, and use Filter and Group to narrow long lists. 3. Edit a page and save Click a page, change the text, then click Save . To add a new page, open the section and click New . For docs pages, Position in the sidebar decides the order lower numbers first , and Short sidebar name is an optional shorter name for the sidebar. A new docs page appears in its section's sidebar automatically. 4. Publish Saving creates a draft. Open the Workflow view the icon at the top left , then move the change from Draft to In review so someone can check it, and to Ready when it is approved. Publishing merges it, and the website updates a few minutes later. !INFO Blog post status A blog post's Status field is separate from publishing. Only posts with Status published are listed on the website, so a post can be merged while staying hidden as draft . Special blocks In the page content, open Insert in the toolbar to add these blocks. This page uses each of them, so you can see what they look like. Callout box A highlighted box that stands out from the text. Pick a kind: !TIP Tip A helpful shortcut or good practice. Shown in green. !INFO Note Background information that is useful but not essential. Shown in blue. !WARNING Warning Something that can go wrong, such as a step that deletes data. Shown in amber. Link cards A grid of clickable boxes, each one leading to another page, with a title and a one-line description. Use them on overview pages so readers can pick what to read next. Each card needs a Title , the page it Links to for example /docs/guides/troubleshooting and an optional Description : cards - Quick start /docs/getting-started : Install OpenFlows and run your first issue. - Troubleshooting /docs/guides/troubleshooting : Fix the most common problems. Numbered steps Write a heading that starts with a number and a full stop, such as 1. Sign in . It is shown with a round number badge, like the headings at the top of this page. Diagram A drawing made from a few lines of text, using Mermaid https://mermaid.js.org . For example, flowchart LR followed by Issue -- Plan -- Review -- Merge draws: mermaid title="An issue moving through OpenFlows" flowchart LR Issue -- Plan -- Review -- Merge Try a diagram at mermaid.live https://mermaid.live first, then paste the text into the block. Images Use the image button in the toolbar, or the Cover image field on blog posts. Uploaded files are stored with the website and get a web-safe name automatically.

title: Contributor Guide
summary: OpenFlows is an open project, and contributions are welcome. Every contribution - whether it’s a bug report, a documentation improvement, or a new feature - flows through a…
text: OpenFlows is an open project, and contributions are welcome. Every contribution - whether it’s a bug report, a documentation improvement, or a new feature - flows through a workflow that mirrors the product’s own culture: a plan or proposal is discussed and agreed before implementation, the change is reviewed, and only reviewed work is merged. Ways to contribute - Report an issue. Found a bug, a confusing behavior, or something that doesn’t match the documentation? Open an issue describing what you observed and what you expected. - Propose a feature. Describe the problem you’re solving and the behavior you’d want to see, and note which existing role or flow it relates to. - Fix a bug or ship a feature. Individual work items are usually scoped as focused changes, each reviewed before merging. - Improve documentation. Accurate, user-facing docs matter - a doc improvement is a real contribution. The contribution workflow 1. Check existing work. Look through open issues and pull requests to avoid duplicating effort. 2. Discuss a non-trivial change first. For larger features, open an issue or start a discussion to align on the approach before writing code. 3. Make a focused change. Keep your change scoped to a clear unit of work. Smaller, reviewable changes move faster than large rewrites. 4. Keep quality high. Follow the project’s conventions and make sure any behavior changes are covered as appropriate. 5. Open a pull request. Explain what you changed and why, and reference the issue it addresses. 6. Address review feedback. Maintainers and the project’s own review culture may request adjustments before merging. !INFO The workflow fits the product OpenFlows practices what its own architecture preaches. A plan or proposal is discussed and agreed before implementation, the change is reviewed, and only reviewed work is merged. Your contribution flows through that same gate-based culture. The project follows an architecture-first, review-before-merge process, and releases are versioned in a controlled way; the documentation website you are reading is part of the project and is published automatically from its main branch, so the docs you see track the current state of the codebase. Governance at a glance How decisions are made: - Small, focused changes move quickly: open, review, merge. - Non-trivial features are discussed and aligned on before implementation, so the approach is agreed before code is written - mirroring the planning gate. - Security-sensitive work gets extra care, consistent with the product's "when in doubt, don't approve" posture. - Maintainers review and merge contributions and steward the architecture; contributors propose and build improvements; users surface issues and ideas that drive direction. For a working local environment, testing expectations, and the release model, see the pages in this section. What makes a good contribution - Clear scope - one problem, one coherent change. - Aligns with the architecture - respects the split between Coder where work runs and OpenFlows how it coordinates , and the security-by-design rules. - Reviewed with the product’s own standards in mind - quality, security, and test coverage matter. Start small, align early, and iterate - that’s the most reliable path to a merge. In this section - Development Setup /docs/contributing/development-setup - get a local environment working. - Adding Skills /docs/contributing/adding-skills - contributing capability content without code. - Testing /docs/contributing/testing - how changes are verified before merging.

title: Testing
summary: Testing is a non-negotiable part of contributing to OpenFlows. The project's standard is simple: changes are verified before they are considered done, and a change is only merged…
text: Testing is a non-negotiable part of contributing to OpenFlows. The project's standard is simple: changes are verified before they are considered done, and a change is only merged once it passes review and its tests are green. This page explains the testing culture and what is expected of every contribution. The standard Before a change is marked complete, it must pass the project's test/build checks. A failing check means the work is not finished - you fix it, or you flag it as blocked rather than working around the failure. This mirrors the product's own posture: verification comes first, and a result that isn't verifiable is not treated as done. What runs The project provides a single, repeatable way to run its checks. In practice that means running the project's test suite or, for the website, a production build from scratch if a build step is part of the check. The exact command is documented in the repository's tooling and the README , and contributors are expected to run it and see it pass before opening or updating a pull request. What is expected of you - Run the checks before you submit. Don't rely on review to catch what a quick local run would find. - Keep behavior changes covered. If your change alters how something behaves, it should be covered by an appropriate test. - Don't cheat the gate. Never mark work complete against failing or broken tests, and don't silently work around a failure. - Keep changes scoped.
