title: Stop Babysitting Your IDE: Why the Future of AI Development Is Asynchronous
summary: Interactive AI chat in your IDE is not autonomous engineering; it is high-speed dictation. It tethers developers to prompt windows and breaks deep work. OpenFlows replaces…
text: Watch how most developers currently work with AI tools like Cursor or GitHub Copilot. An engineer opens their IDE. They highlight a function, type a prompt into a sidebar, and sit watching the model generate code line by line. The model hallucinates an import. The engineer types another prompt: "No, use our internal logging package." The model fixes that import, but accidentally breaks a unit test. The engineer types a third prompt: "Fix the broken test." Two hours later, the engineer has written twenty prompts, babysat a chat window, and made minimal architectural progress. The industry calls this "AI productivity." In reality, it is high-speed dictation. It keeps developers trapped in synchronous, low-leverage manual labor. It fractures concentration, interrupts flow state, and still requires a human engineer to sit at the keyboard guiding every keystroke. The Synchronous Chat Trap Synchronous chat assistants create three major problems for engineering teams: 1. Context Switching and Fatigue: Prompt-and-wait workflows destroy deep work. An engineer waiting 20 to 45 seconds for an LLM response gets distracted, checks Slack or email, and loses their train of thought. 2. Linear Human Bottlenecks: A developer can only chat with one assistant at a time. The work does not scale beyond the engineer's active hours at their keyboard. 3. Lack of Team Alignment: Chat threads live inside individual IDE windows. The prompts, context, and failed attempts are invisible to the rest of the team. There is no shared queue, no reproducible history, and no team-wide governance. Real software engineering at scale has never worked synchronously. A technical lead does not stand behind a software engineer's desk dictating every line of code as they type. The lead creates a clear ticket, documents architectural boundaries, defines acceptance criteria, and assigns the task. The engineer works independently, runs tests, and opens a pull request for review. If human software teams operate through asynchronous issue queues and code reviews, why are we forcing AI agents into synchronous chat boxes? What Makes OpenFlows Different: The Asynchronous AI Dev Team OpenFlows replaces interactive chat with an asynchronous, issue-driven workflow. Instead of prompting an IDE extension line by line, you direct an autonomous team of specialized agents through your existing GitHub issues. Here is how the workflow operates: 1. You Define Intent, Not Syntax You open a GitHub issue in your repository. You describe the feature or bug fix, mention the files involved, and list the acceptance criteria. Once submitted, your job as an architect is done. You close your laptop and move on to other priorities. 2. Specialized Agents Coordinate Autonomously Instead of a single model trying to do everything inside one prompt window, OpenFlows coordinates a team of five specialized agents: - NEXUS Orchestrator : Detects the new issue, provisions an isolated Coder workspace, and allocates the task. - FORGE Builder : Analyzes the codebase, drafts an architectural contract CONTRACT.md , and implements the code changes in small, verified segments. - SENTINEL Reviewer : Reviews the implementation against the contract, executes tests in an isolated verification sandbox, and checks for edge cases and regressions. - VESSEL DevOps : Monitors CI runs, resolves rebase conflicts, and manages branch hygiene. - LORE Documenter : Updates release notes, documentation, and changelogs. 3. Ephemeral Workspaces with Zero Idle Waste Every task runs inside its own disposable, containerized workspace on your infrastructure. The agents do not touch your personal laptop or share dirty working trees. Once the pull request is merged, the workspace is destroyed. 4. Review Finished Work, Not Half-Baked Drafts When you open GitHub the next morning, you do not find a chat transcript. You find a complete, tested pull request with: - Passing unit and integration tests. - A written architectural plan explaining what changed and why. - An adversarial review sign-off from SENTINEL. - A clean git history ready for merge. Moving from Doing to Directing Generative AI should not turn software engineers into full-time prompt typists. The real leverage of AI comes when engineers step into the role of architects: defining system requirements, enforcing standards, and letting an autonomous team handle execution in the background. Stop babysitting chat boxes in your editor. Let your AI team work asynchronously.

title: The Agent That Deleted Production Was Not the Root Cause
summary: An autonomous coding agent deletes a production database from a developer's machine.
text: Months later, someone opens an issue: add a safeguard, improve the prompt, prevent the agent from running that command again. By then, the most important question has already been missed. Why did a coding agent on a developer machine have credentials capable of deleting a production database in the first place? The immediate failure may have been an incorrect command. The systemic failure happened earlier, when the infrastructure gave one runtime enough authority to build, approve, and operate production without meaningful boundaries. Autonomous agents are not inherently the problem. But autonomy amplifies the design of the environment around it. A carefully constrained agent can be useful and predictable. An agent with a developer's complete credentials, broad network access, and no independent reviewer is simply an unbounded production principal that happens to communicate in natural language. That is not an agent architecture. It is a permissions accident waiting for an incident report. Human access is not an agent permission model The easiest way to deploy an engineering agent is to give it the same environment as a developer: the developer's shell, GitHub session, cloud credentials, Kubernetes context, password manager, and access to production. It is also the most dangerous way. A human stakeholder may legitimately carry several responsibilities. A senior engineer can write code, review an emergency change, operate infrastructure, and communicate with the organization. Those powers are moderated by context, social accountability, fatigue, judgment, and organizational process. An agent runtime should not inherit that complete role merely because it runs on the human's machine. The correct question is not, “What can the developer do?” It is, “What is the smallest set of actions this agent needs for this specific responsibility?” The answer should be encoded in infrastructure, not left to a system prompt. The builder must not be both judge and jury The most important boundary is not between humans and agents. It is between responsibilities. An agent that writes a change should not be the only agent that decides whether the change is correct. It has the same context, assumptions, and blind spots that produced the implementation. Asking it to review itself often produces a more articulate version of its original reasoning, not an independent assessment. The builder can and should run tests. It should inspect its diff, check formatting, and catch obvious mistakes. But those checks are evidence supplied to a review process; they are not the final verdict. Independent validation matters for the same reason that independent code review matters in a human organization. The reviewer must be able to reject the work. The rejection must return the work to the builder. The builder must not be able to approve its own plan, manufacture its own review decision, or bypass a failed gate. In other words: an agent should never be both the judged and the jury of its own work. How OpenFlows separates authority OpenFlows divides the software-delivery lifecycle among agents with distinct responsibilities: - NEXUS coordinates work, assigns tickets, recovers stalled flows, and handles human escalation. - FORGE plans and implements changes on an assigned branch. - SENTINEL independently reviews plans, runs verification against the builder's exact candidate commit, and approves or rejects the result. - VESSEL evaluates merge readiness, CI, conflicts, and deployment conditions before merging or operating infrastructure. - LORE handles documentation work through its own bounded repository profile. These are not decorative personas. Each role receives a different permission profile and occupies a different position in an enforced state machine. The normal lifecycle is: text planning - plan ready - building - testing - submit - done FORGE can submit a plan, but it cannot approve that plan and move itself into implementation. SENTINEL's approval performs that transition. FORGE can produce a candidate commit, but SENTINEL verifies and approves the exact revision and commit before the flow enters submission. VESSEL merges only after the required review and current-head CI evidence are present. Rejection is a real state transition, not a comment that the builder is free to ignore. Frozen phases prevent source changes while a candidate is being reviewed. A blocked flow recovers through planning instead of jumping directly back into implementation. Review rounds and commit identities are recorded so an approval for an old head cannot silently authorize a new one. This matters because prompts are advisory. State transitions, credential boundaries, and denied operations are enforceable. Least privilege must exist at token issuance OpenFlows does not hand every workspace a broad GitHub credential and ask the agent to use it carefully. The Manager acts as a credential broker. It knows the workspace, tenant, repository, installation, and stored agent role. A runtime may request only a coarse purpose: Git transport or API access. It cannot choose its own repository or submit a custom permission set. The Manager resolves a server-controlled, versioned profile. Unknown roles fail closed. The current profiles are deliberately different: Agent Git access API access Intended responsibility --- --- --- --- NEXUS Contents: read Contents: read; issues and pull requests: write Discover and coordinate work without implementing repository changes FORGE Contents and workflows: write Contents and pull requests: write Implement, push the assigned branch, and create or update its pull request SENTINEL Contents: read Contents and checks: read; pull requests: write Inspect code and CI, then submit independent review feedback VESSEL Contents: write Contents and pull requests: write; checks, statuses, and actions: read Perform approved merge and delivery operations using current CI evidence LORE Contents: write Contents and pull requests: write…

title: No More "My Agent Did This Without Me Knowing": Bringing Engineering Discipline Back to AI
summary: Every developer now runs an ad-hoc AI agent on their laptop with zero shared protocols or governance. The result is shadow engineering: "my agent broke that without me knowing."…
text: Every software engineering team has experienced some version of this morning standup over the last six months: "Wait, who modified the authentication middleware?" "Oh, sorry, my agent refactored that in the background while I was prompting it on the user profile ticket. I did not realize it touched that file." Or: "Why did CI fail on main?" "My local agent ran a migration script on its own. It worked on my laptop." Sound familiar? Overnight, engineering organizations that spent decades building rigorous continuous integration, security policies, and pull request rituals have devolved into the Wild West. Every engineer has their own agent, their own command-line wrapper, their own prompts, their own system permissions, and their own unvetted conventions running directly on their personal machine. We call it "AI-assisted development," but let us be honest about what it really is: shadow engineering without a protocol. Software development has never been done this way before AI came along. And there is a very good reason for that. The 40 Years of Discipline We Conveniently Forgot Before the generative AI boom, no credible engineering team would have tolerated a workflow where: 1. Individual developers invent their own proprietary build and test protocols on their local machines. 2. Unreviewed code is written without a prior architectural spec or agreed definition of done. 3. Untrusted processes execute arbitrary shell commands with root privileges and ambient access to .env secrets, production tokens, and SSH keys. 4. Coworkers bypass code review and push straight to shared branches. We spent four decades establishing industry-wide invariants: - Reproducible, isolated environments so we never hear "it works on my machine" again. - Specification and contract-first design before writing code. - Adversarial peer review where the reviewer cannot be coerced by the author. - Least-privilege execution where tools only have access to what they strictly need. Yet when AI agents arrived, the industry threw those hard-won lessons out the window. We handed autonomous LLMs full write access to local file systems, gave them terminal access, prompted them with vague natural language, and hoped for the best. When things inevitably break, developers shrug: "My agent did it without me knowing." That is not autonomous software engineering. That is chaos with a high token bill. The Trap of the Uncoordinated Local Agent The problem is not that AI models are incapable of writing code. Models can write excellent code when given a crisp, bounded specification. The problem is a complete lack of orchestration protocols and environmental governance. When every engineer runs an uncoordinated agent on their own laptop: - No Shared State: Agent A knows nothing about what Agent B is touching. They step on each other's toes, collide on branch changes, and duplicate effort. - Unchecked Hallucination: Without an adversarial review gate before code is written, an agent will happily invent non-existent APIs, pull in hallucinated dependencies, and drift away from team architectural patterns. - Credential Leakage: When an agent runs locally, your company's API keys, database credentials, and internal secrets sit in plain view of third-party model context windows. - No Auditable Trail: When an unexpected commit lands, nobody knows what prompt triggered it, what invariants were checked, or whether a human ever approved it. If a human junior engineer worked this way refactoring random modules without a ticket, skipping peer review, and running unvetted scripts with production keys , they would be removed from the repository within an hour. Why are we holding AI agents to a lower standard than our interns? How OpenFlows Takes Us Back on Track OpenFlows was built on a simple premise: AI development should elevate engineering discipline, not erode it. Instead of letting agents run loose on personal laptops, OpenFlows brings back the battle-tested patterns of real software teams. The entire architecture rests on one foundational asymmetry: Coder governs WHERE agents run. OpenFlows governs HOW agents coordinate. Here is the exact lifecycle OpenFlows enforces for every single task: 1. GitHub Issue received: An issue lands in the repository. 2. NEXUS Orchestrator : Picks it up, provisions an isolated Coder workspace, and allocates the ticket. 3. FORGE Builder - Planning mode : Analyzes the issue and drafts CONTRACT.md . Zero source files are touched. 4. Gated Checkpoint: SENTINEL reviews and signs off on the plan before any code can be modified. 5. FORGE Builder - Coding mode : Implements code strictly against the agreed contract on a dedicated branch. 6. SENTINEL Reviewer : Performs adversarial review and runs delegated verification tests via the A2A Relay. 7. VESSEL DevOps : Confirms passing CI, merges the PR, and cleans up the disposable workspace. 1. Governed, Ephemeral Workspaces No More "My Machine" OpenFlows agents never run in your personal terminal or on your local machine. They run inside disposable, enterprise-governed Coder workspaces. - Worker containers have zero AI software and zero LLM API keys . LLM routing is handled centrally through Coder's AI Gateway. - When the task is done and the PR is merged, the workspace is destroyed. No lingering background processes, no phantom file changes. 2. Gated Planning Before Any Code is Written In OpenFlows, FORGE the builder is strictly prohibited from touching source code until it produces a CONTRACT.md detailing the files to modify, the data flow, and the test strategy. - SENTINEL the reviewer must inspect, challenge, and approve the plan. - If there is ambiguity or a security question, the system halts and escalates to a human. - No agent ever refactors code without you knowing, because the plan is locked before the first line is committed. 3. Adversarial Verification via the A2A Protocol Having an agent review its own code is like letting a student grade their own exam. In…

title: Don’t Build on Vibes. Build on Architecture.
summary: AI can generate code quickly, but reliable software needs more than suggestions. OpenFlows helps teams turn architectural intent into governed, secure, production-ready delivery.
text: AI has made writing code faster than ever. That is useful, but it has also created a risky habit: building software from prompts, vibes, and whichever suggestion an AI produces next A feature request becomes a chat. A chat becomes code. Code becomes a pull request. Somewhere along the way, the architecture disappears. The result may feel productive at first. Without deliberate design, however, teams inherit inconsistency, fragile integrations, unclear ownership, security gaps, and systems that become harder to evolve with every release. Software is not only code generation. It is architecture, decisions, boundaries, workflows, security, product intent, and accountability. That is why OpenFlows exists. Own the architecture. Own the software. OpenFlows is built on a simple principle: you should own your architecture, your software, and the way it is produced. You define the direction. You impose the design. You choose the constraints, standards, technology, security posture, and engineering practices that matter to your organisation. OpenFlows then turns that direction into delivery. Instead of asking an AI to build something nice, you interact with a governed system. Think of it more like working with a compiler than gambling with a chatbot. You provide the inputs, rules, and architectural intent. OpenFlows coordinates the work needed to produce an implementation that follows them. Your architecture becomes the source of truth. Your software is the output. From AI suggestions to engineered delivery AI suggestions are easy to get. Engineering discipline is harder. A generic coding assistant can propose code, explain an API, or generate a component. It does not automatically understand your domain boundaries, your team’s conventions, your deployment model, your security controls, or the trade-offs behind a technical decision. Those things must be designed. OpenFlows brings agentic development into an architecture-first workflow. It coordinates specialised AI roles across planning, implementation, testing, review, and verification, inside controlled development environments and existing engineering workflows. The goal is not to remove engineers from the process. The goal is to reduce the friction between architectural intent and reliable software delivery. With OpenFlows, teams can: - Define work through their existing GitHub workflow. - Establish architecture and engineering constraints before code is written. - Use planning and review checkpoints to keep work accountable. - Run AI agents in isolated, governed environments. - Produce reviewed pull requests rather than disconnected snippets of code. - Keep humans in control of the decisions that shape the product. This is how AI becomes useful at scale: not as an uncontrolled source of suggestions, but as a system that executes within a design you own. Your design. Your pace. Your taste. Every engineering organisation has its own way of building. Some value speed above all else. Others operate under strict security, compliance, or infrastructure requirements. Some need strong architectural governance across multiple teams. Others want to move quickly without losing the quality that makes future growth possible. OpenFlows is designed for that reality. You choose the design. You determine the pace. You set the standards. Whether your approach is pragmatic and lightweight or highly structured and controlled, the system should serve your engineering culture. It should not replace it with someone else’s assumptions. That is what makes agentic development compatible with real software architecture. Architecture is no longer a document that becomes outdated. It is an active constraint on how software is planned, built, tested, reviewed, and shipped. Automated does not mean uncontrolled The future of software development is not an AI agent with unrestricted access to production systems. It is an automated delivery system with clear boundaries. OpenFlows supports that model with isolated workspaces, defined responsibilities, planning gates, adversarial review, auditable workflows, and a clear separation between the environment where work runs and the flow that governs how agents collaborate. Automation should increase confidence, not reduce it. Governance should enable speed, not become bureaucracy. Security should be part of the delivery model, not an afterthought once code has been generated. When those pieces work together, teams move faster because they no longer have to choose between velocity and control. Ship faster without surrendering the system The promise of agentic development is not simply that code can be written faster. The real promise is that teams can shorten the distance between a well-considered decision and a production-ready change. OpenFlows helps make that possible. You own the architecture. You own the software. You impose the design. OpenFlows helps produce the result at your speed, with your standards, and according to your taste. Stop building from vibes. Build from architecture.

title: The Forge-Sentinel Pair: Software Engineering as a Disposable Two-Player Team
summary:
Every software engineer knows the shape of a good workday. You don't walk in, wave your
hands, and hope the code appears. You clock in, read the ticket, think about the data flow,…
text: The Forge-Sentinel pair is that workday, automated. Two agents, FORGE the builder and SENTINEL the reviewer, are provisioned as a 1:1 pair to complete exactly one task. They are armed with a curated arsenal of commands, skills, hooks, and tools that force the work to happen architecturally rather than by feel. And when the task is done, the whole thing workspaces, state, locks, context is destroyed, leaving only a merged PR and a clean slot ready for the next ticket. This is not another "autonomous coding agent" demo. It's a discipline. Let's walk through how the pair operates. One ticket, one pair, one branch Before either agent does anything, NEXUS the orchestrator takes a GitHub issue and assigns it to an idle pair slot. That assignment is a promise of full isolation: - Each pair gets its own Git worktree on its own branch forge-pair-1/T-42 . Two pairs never share a checkout, never touch the same branch. - Each pair gets its own shared/ directory : the only channel where FORGE and SENTINEL talk to each other. Tickets, plans, contracts, evaluations all live there. - Dynamic file locks guarantee two pairs can't stomp the same file even when scope grows. The pair is scoped to the task from the moment it's born. FORGE cannot see what forge-2 is doing. It has no reason to. Its entire universe is TICKET.md , its worktree, and the shared directory where SENTINEL will reply. Armed with curated commands and skills, not vibes A pair is only as reliable as its tooling. Neither agent is handed a blank chat and told "go figure it out." Each is provisioned with a purpose-built orchestration plugin : skills, hooks, slash commands, and MCP servers that encode how the work gets done. And crucially, this arsenal is not static. It compounds over time . Every hard-won lesson from the engineering organization is folded back into the plugin: battle-tested skills, refined design principles, coding standards, architecture patterns, API contracts, and review guidelines. Each new ticket the pair runs is executed against the accumulated experience of every ticket before it. FORGE doesn't rediscover "how we write async error handling here" on its own, and SENTINEL doesn't re-learn "what an acceptable PR looks like." That knowledge is codified and handed to them at session start. The pair is armed with a living, growing playbook, not a one-off prompt. Skills: injected knowledge, not prompt bloat On session start, each agent receives the skills relevant to its role as reference documents: - FORGE loads forge-planning and forge-coding , the discipline of writing a plan before code, sizing segments 1–3 files, 20–40 minutes , and testing every new function. - SENTINEL loads sentinel-review and sentinel-criteria , the five evaluation criteria correctness, test coverage, standards compliance, code quality, no regressions that every approval must pass. The skills don't make the agents capable ; they make them consistent . FORGE doesn't wonder whether it should test; the skill says every new function needs a test, and the hook enforces it. Hooks: invariants the agent cannot bypass Skills are suggestions; hooks are law. Lifecycle hooks run around every action and refuse to let the agent skip the process: - FORGE : a pre write check hook enforces file ownership locks before every write; a post write lint hook runs the linter on every changed file; a pre bash guard blocks dangerous commands like direct git push ; a stop require artifact hook refuses to let FORGE exit until it has produced a valid STATUS.json or HANDOFF.md . - SENTINEL : a pre bash readonly guard makes the reviewer read-only against source. It can run tests and linters but cannot modify a single line of FORGE's code; a stop require eval hook refuses exit until an evaluation is written. The message is blunt: you don't get to leave until the work is finished and recorded. That's the equivalent of an engineer being told the ticket isn't done until the PR is up and the tests are green. Commands: structured procedures Slash commands bundle multi-step procedures so the agent doesn't improvise the workflow: - /plan : reads the ticket, searches the codebase for existing patterns, and writes a structured PLAN.md with segment breakdown and definition of done. - /segment-done : runs the full test suite, lints changed files, commits the segment, and notifies SENTINEL. - /handoff : writes a complete handoff and exits cleanly when context runs low. - /status : verifies the final review is approved, pushes the branch, opens the PR via the GitHub MCP server, and records the terminal STATUS.json . MCP servers: external capability, scoped Rather than build a custom tool binary, the pair is wired to battle-tested MCP servers GitHub, Redis, filesystem, shell , each scoped to the pair's own worktree and credentials. FORGE can open a PR through GitHub MCP; the shell server only allows an explicit allowlist run-tests.sh , cargo test , eslint , ruff . The agent gets real capability with constraints that make it safe to run unattended. The gated workflow: planning → building → reviewing The pair's rhythm is a series of hard gates . FORGE cannot skip ahead, and SENTINEL cannot approve without evidence. 1. The planning gate FORGE reads the ticket, searches the codebase for existing patterns, and writes PLAN.md : its understanding of the ticket, the technical approach, an explicit segment breakdown, a testable definition of done per segment, and an out-of-scope list. It then sets status set planning and halts . The harness watches the shared directory and, on seeing the plan, spawns a fresh SENTINEL to review it before a single line of code is written . SENTINEL checks whether the plan addresses every acceptance criterion, whether the approach follows the codebase's architecture patterns, and whether the definition of done is actually testable. It writes CONTRACT.md : either AGREED or a list of specific objections. If there are objections, the plan goes back. After three rounds of…

title: The AI Dev Team vs Human Dev Team: Why Orchestration Beats Sequential Prompting
summary: AI gets expensive when a human sits at a keyboard, prompt after prompt, wrangling a machine into production-ready code through sequential conversation. Orchestration changes the…
text: AI is expensive when you have a human sitting at a keyboard, prompt after prompt, trying to wrangle a machine into producing production-ready code through sequential conversation. Both parties lack a shared conceptual framework for the process. The human says "build me a login system," the AI produces something, the human says "no, not like that," and the cycle repeats burning tokens, burning time, burning money. That's not AI development. That's AI tourism. But there's another way. One where AI doesn't replace developers it amplifies them. Where humans move from the doing to the directing, and machines handle the execution with precision. The Real Equation: Human Architecture × AI Execution The difference between an expensive AI experiment and a cost-effective AI team isn't the model it's the orchestration. Think about it: a senior software architect doesn't write every line of code themselves. They define the patterns, set the conventions, review the work, and ensure quality. What if we could apply that same principle to AI? Here's what happens when you get it right: - Speed: An orchestrated AI team works in parallel, not sequentially - Cost: Clear specifications mean fewer iterations, fewer tokens, less waste - Quality: Multiple review gates catch issues before they become expensive problems - Consistency: Defined conventions prevent the creative drift that plagues solo AI development The bottleneck isn't AI capability it's human-AI coordination. Where Solo AI Development Fails As a software engineer who has built both with and without AI, I've seen the pattern repeat: 1. Creative Hallucination: AI is brilliantly creative too creative. Without guardrails, it invents patterns that don't exist in your codebase 2. Convention Drift: Start with clean code, end with a Frankenstein monster of styles and approaches 3. Context Collapse: The bigger the project, the more the AI loses the thread 4. Token Burn: Each correction cycle costs money. Ten correction cycles cost a fortune These aren't AI problems. They're process problems. read https://medium.com/@yemelechristian2/the-ai-dev-team-vs-human-dev-team-why-orchestration-beats-sequential-prompting-45eda0742002

title: Delegated Verification: How SENTINEL Gets FORGE to Run Code, Without Ever Touching FORGE's Workspace
summary: A design for cross-workspace command execution that lets a reviewer agent verify code by asking for evidence - never by entering the workspace it's reviewing.
text: The problem: a reviewer that can't run the tests SENTINEL's job is to gate FORGE's work at two points: reviewing PLAN.md before implementation starts, and reviewing the PR before it merges. Both of those reviews are, today, read-only - SENTINEL reads an artifact a plan, a diff and reasons about it. That's fine for "does this plan make sense" or "is this diff internally consistent." It falls apart for a very ordinary question: does the code actually work? Answering that requires running something - cargo test , npm test , a lint pass, a build. And that command has to run somewhere with the repository checked out, which today means it has to run inside FORGE's Coder workspace, not SENTINEL's. The naive fix - give SENTINEL shell access to FORGE's workspace - was rejected for three reasons that all come back to the same principle: the reviewer must remain isolated from the thing it reviews. - It breaks the review's integrity. A reviewer that can mutate the artifact it's reviewing intentionally, or via a prompt-injected ticket is not a reviewer anymore. - It couples SENTINEL's lifecycle to FORGE's workspace. If FORGE's workspace is torn down, gone, or mid-provisioning, SENTINEL loses a capability it needs for something as basic as approving a gate. - Coder workspaces don't share a filesystem see the "no shared filesystem across workspaces" discussion in OpenFlows Coder Integrated Architecture.md , so this would have meant inventing a new cross-workspace mount just to serve one use case. The design that shipped instead: SENTINEL never enters FORGE's workspace. It delegates . It sends FORGE a typed request - "run this command, tell me what happened" - and gets back a structured result. FORGE stays the only thing that touches its own filesystem. SENTINEL stays a pure reviewer, just one that can now ask for evidence instead of only reading claims. Why A2A, and why not just reuse Redis OpenFlows already has a cross-workspace coordination mechanism: the Redis SharedStore, accessed exclusively through openflows-harness . PLAN.md lives there as pair: id :plan ; handoffs, PR info, and review verdicts all live there too. So the obvious question is: why introduce a second protocol A2A instead of just writing a "please run this command" key to Redis and polling for the answer? The two mechanisms are solving genuinely different problems, and conflating them would have made both worse: Redis SharedStore A2A --- --- --- Nature Durable artifact store Live task/message exchange Good at "What is the current plan?" "What did the review say?" - anything that should survive a restart and be replayed/audited "Go do this now, stream me progress, tell me when it's done" Semantics Poll-and-read Request/response with SSE streaming, cancellation, resubscribe-after-disconnect Ecosystem Bespoke, tenant-namespaced keys Standard task lifecycle, Agent Cards, JSON-RPC methods with existing tooling A verify request is fundamentally a task , not a fact . It has a lifecycle - submitted, running, producing incremental output, completing or timing out - that Redis's plain-key model can express, but only by reinventing exactly what A2A already standardizes task IDs, progress streaming, cancellation, resubscription . Doing that with hand-rolled Redis polling would have produced a bespoke pseudo-A2A with worse ergonomics and no compatible tooling. So the design draws a firm line: Redis remains the single source of truth for durable artifacts. A2A is used only for live task exchange, and every terminal A2A result is mirrored into Redis before the task is acknowledged complete. That second sentence matters as much as the first: A2A doesn't get to be a second, competing source of truth. The moment a verify task finishes, its result is written to pair: id :verification in Redis - so even though the conversation happened over A2A, the record lives in the same durable store as everything else, replayable and auditable the same way a PR or a plan is. Why a relay, not peer-to-peer Given A2A for the live exchange, the next question is topology: does SENTINEL dial FORGE directly, or does something sit in between? Coder workspaces are reliably good at making outbound connections and bad at accepting inbound ones - there's no stable address for "the FORGE workspace for pair T-048" that SENTINEL could dial, short of wiring up coder app URLs and a discovery mechanism for every pair. So the design puts a relay inside nexus , the existing control-plane workspace, and has both SENTINEL and FORGE open outbound connections to it. Nexus routes messages by pair id, role . This isn't just a networking convenience. It's the enforcement point: - Authorization - nexus is the only place that knows the pair's role map, so it's the only place that can refuse a request from a SENTINEL trying to address a FORGE outside its own pair. - Command allowlisting - nexus rejects verify requests whose command doesn't match a known-safe prefix cargo test , npm test , etc. before it ever reaches an executor. Rejections are logged to audit:a2a:rejected . - Audit - every accepted request and its result gets a durable trail, because nexus is the chokepoint that writes it. - A single kill switch - if something goes wrong with delegated verification as a feature, there's one relay to disable, not N peer connections. The alternative - SENTINEL and FORGE dialing each other directly once nexus hands out short-lived tokens - was considered and explicitly deferred. It solves nothing that the relay doesn't already solve for v1, and it adds a token-exchange and NAT-traversal problem that isn't worth taking on before the simpler design has been proven. What actually gets sent The whole capability rests on one task type: verify . It's deliberately narrow - not "run any shell command," but "run this specific, allowlisted command and tell me what happened": jsonc // SENTINEL → nexus → FORGE "task type": "verify", "pair id": "T-048", "verify": "kind": "command", "cwd": "repo", "argv":…

title: OpenFlows State Machine
summary: OpenFlows uses a durable state machine to control autonomous software delivery. The state machine defines how work moves from intent to merge, which approvals are required, which…
text: System Context OpenFlows runs an agent team across governed workspaces. Each agent has a role: - NEXUS coordinates assignment, routing, and recovery. - FORGE plans and builds the change. - SENTINEL reviews plans, implementation, and verification evidence. - VESSEL merges only approved and verified work. - Human operators approve high-trust gates before submission and merge. The state machine is the shared authority across those roles. It prevents each agent from treating local memory, chat history, GitHub state, or workspace status as the source of truth. Those systems remain projections. The lifecycle record is the control point. Lifecycle Graph mermaid stateDiagram-v2 -- planning planning -- plan ready: upload and submit plan plan ready -- plan rejected: SENTINEL rejects plan rejected -- planning: revise plan ready -- building: SENTINEL approves exact revision and round building -- testing: commit and clean checkout testing -- building: failed review or rework testing -- submit: A2A evidence, SENTINEL approval, human approval submit -- building: PR or CI rejection, changed head submit -- done: SENTINEL approval, human approval, CI success, confirmed merge blocked -- planning: recover done -- Lifecycle Phases Planning Planning is the entry phase for active work. FORGE converts a ticket into an explicit plan. The plan is not treated as advisory context. It becomes versioned lifecycle data. Any return to planning means the prior downstream evidence is no longer trusted. Plan Ready Plan ready means the plan has been submitted for review. SENTINEL evaluates the plan before implementation begins. This phase separates architectural agreement from code generation. It blocks premature construction and forces design intent to be reviewed while it is still cheap to change. Plan Rejected Plan rejected means SENTINEL found a material issue in the plan. The only forward motion is back to planning. FORGE must revise and resubmit. The system does not allow a rejected plan to drift into implementation through side channels. Building Building begins only after SENTINEL approves a specific plan revision and review round. FORGE implements against that approved plan. Returning to building from a later phase invalidates testing and PR evidence because the candidate artifact has changed. Testing Testing means there is a candidate commit on a clean checkout. SENTINEL can request verification and review the result against the approved plan. The tested head must remain stable. Dirty, missing, stale, changed, or timed-out evidence cannot authorize progress. Submit Submit means the work has passed implementation review and human approval for the testing phase. A pull request can be opened or updated, CI can run, and final submission gates can be evaluated. The submitted head, review round, PR identity, and evidence remain bound together. Done Done is terminal. It requires a confirmed merge, not merely an approved PR, a green local test, or an optimistic GitHub response. The lifecycle records the actual merge outcome so restart recovery can distinguish completed work from pending or ambiguous work. Blocked Blocked is a controlled interruption for nonterminal work. It records that progress cannot continue under current conditions. Today, recovery is driven by FORGE: once the blocker clears, FORGE moves the lifecycle back to planning blocked → planning because the safest restart point is an explicit re-evaluation of intent and constraints. blocked is not terminal; done is the only absorbing state. Future design: human-driven recovery Planned evolution not yet implemented routes blocked recovery through a human operator rather than relying on FORGE to self-recover: - When status is set to blocked , the controller notifies a human operator with the recorded blocker, exact evidence, and the answerable unblock question. - The human addresses the underlying issue outside the lifecycle repairing infrastructure, providing credentials/approval, resolving an external dependency, or correcting the constraint . - The human then explicitly sets the next phase the machine should resume from typically planning , or building / testing when the blocker was external to the work and downstream evidence remains valid . - The lifecycle record persists the human's phase directive as an audited, actor-tagged transition, and the system resumes from that phase. This keeps blocked as a genuine human checkpoint: no autonomous agent advances out of blocked on its own. The human decision is recorded in the same versioned lifecycle history as every other transition, so restart recovery can distinguish "blocked and awaiting the operator" from "blocked and resolved." Until this is implemented, the current FORGE-driven blocked → planning path remains authoritative. Transition Motions The state machine has three primary motions. Forward motion advances work only when the required evidence for the current phase exists. Planning moves to plan ready when a plan is submitted. Plan ready moves to building only after SENTINEL approves the exact plan revision and review round. Testing moves to submit only after verification, SENTINEL approval, and human approval. Submit moves to done only after final approval, CI success, and confirmed merge. Corrective motion sends work backward when evidence fails or becomes stale. Plan rejection returns to planning. Failed implementation review or verification returns to building. PR rejection, CI failure, or a changed submitted head returns to building. These transitions deliberately discard downstream confidence. Recovery motion handles interruption and ambiguity. Blocked work returns to planning today; in the planned future design a human operator is notified, resolves the issue, and explicitly sets the resume phase before the machine advances. Merge uncertainty does not automatically unlock or retry unsafe operations. The lifecycle preserves reservations and pending deliveries until a safe reconciliation path…

title: Coder Didn't Make OpenFlows Smarter. It Made It Trustworthy.
summary: An orchestrator is only as trustworthy as the runtime underneath it. Coder gave OpenFlows that runtime - and it changed what OpenFlows could promise.

title: NEXUS · Orchestrator
summary: Turns GitHub issues into typed tickets, assigns workers, and runs reconcile() every cycle so nothing stalls silently.
text: Turns GitHub issues into typed tickets, assigns workers, and runs reconcile() every cycle so nothing stalls silently. Focus: Issue sync, Assignment, Recovery. Runs in openflows-nexus workspace. Writes Tickets, assignments, escalations. Never Lets an escalation stall silently.

title: FORGE · Builder
summary: Plans first, then implements segment by segment in an isolated workspace that holds no LLM keys or raw credentials.
text: Plans first, then implements segment by segment in an isolated workspace that holds no LLM keys or raw credentials. Focus: PLAN.md, Commits, Tests. Runs in Ephemeral workspace per ticket. Writes Its own pair branch and PR. Never Holds LLM keys or raw credentials.

title: SENTINEL · Reviewer
summary: Approves the plan gate, reviews every PR adversarially, and verifies by running tests through the A2A relay.
text: Approves the plan gate, reviews every PR adversarially, and verifies by running tests through the A2A relay. Focus: Plan gate, Review, A2A verify. Runs in Fresh, read-only workspace. Writes Gate approvals and verdicts. Never Approves when in doubt.

title: VESSEL · DevOps
summary: Watches CI, catches conflicts early, and squash-merges only PRs that are approved, conflict-free, and green.
text: Watches CI, catches conflicts early, and squash-merges only PRs that are approved, conflict-free, and green. Focus: CI, Conflicts, Merge. Runs in Controller-side monitor. Writes Squash merges into main. Never Force-pushes or bypasses protection.

title: LORE · Documenter
summary: Writes Architecture Decision Records and changelog entries after every merge, so the "why" is never lost.
text: Writes Architecture Decision Records and changelog entries after every merge, so the "why" is never lost. Focus: ADRs, Changelog, Optional. Runs in After every merge event. Writes docs/ only: ADRs, changelog. Never Blocks active development.

title: What is OpenFlows, and how does it relate to Coder?
summary: OpenFlows is an autonomous AI software team that turns GitHub issues into reviewed pull requests. Coder hosts the isolated workspaces where the agents run; OpenFlows decides how…
text: OpenFlows is an autonomous AI software team that turns GitHub issues into reviewed pull requests. Coder hosts the isolated workspaces where the agents run; OpenFlows decides how they coordinate. Manager owns organizations, tenants, workspace lifecycle, runtime identity and credential brokerage, and Nexus coordinates planning, review and delivery inside each tenant.

title: Is OpenFlows open source?
summary: Yes. OpenFlows is MIT licensed and self-hosted on your own Coder environment. You can read the code, run it, change it and contribute .
text: Yes. OpenFlows is MIT licensed and self-hosted on your own Coder environment. You can read the code, run it, change it and contribute .

title: How does an issue become a merged pull request?
summary: NEXUS turns a GitHub issue into a ticket and assigns a FORGE worker. FORGE writes a plan and stops until SENTINEL approves it, then implements it and opens a pull request.…
text: NEXUS turns a GitHub issue into a ticket and assigns a FORGE worker. FORGE writes a plan and stops until SENTINEL approves it, then implements it and opens a pull request. SENTINEL reviews the change, VESSEL merges it once checks pass, and LORE records what was decided. See How OpenFlows works .

title: Do I still review the code?
summary: You decide how much. Humans own the issues, the specs and the gates that need a person, and every pull request stays reviewable on GitHub. When an agent hits an ambiguous spec or…
text: You decide how much. Humans own the issues, the specs and the gates that need a person, and every pull request stays reviewable on GitHub. When an agent hits an ambiguous spec or an unresolvable conflict, the ticket is escalated to a human instead of guessed at.

title: How much does OpenFlows cost to run?
summary: OpenFlows itself is free. Your cost is your own infrastructure and model usage. You control it by choosing a model per role, for example a more careful model for the reviewer and…
text: OpenFlows itself is free. Your cost is your own infrastructure and model usage. You control it by choosing a model per role, for example a more careful model for the reviewer and a general coding model for the builder.

title: Which models can OpenFlows use?
summary: You enable models in the Coder AI settings and assign one to each role in the agent registry. Calls go through your own model gateway in the control plane, so you choose which…
text: You enable models in the Coder AI settings and assign one to each role in the agent registry. Calls go through your own model gateway in the control plane, so you choose which models your team can use and can switch a role to another model without a restart.

title: Where do AI calls happen?
summary: Model access follows the configured Coder and agent runtime settings. Manager brokers infrastructure credentials. A workspace can receive a scoped bootstrap bundle and short-lived…
text: Model access follows the configured Coder and agent runtime settings. Manager brokers infrastructure credentials. A workspace can receive a scoped bootstrap bundle and short-lived GitHub installation tokens. See the credential flow .

title: Is my code sent to third parties?
summary: Code is available to the workspace and to the model provider you configure. GitHub also receives repository API and Git traffic. Review the provider, Coder and GitHub data paths…
text: Code is available to the workspace and to the model provider you configure. GitHub also receives repository API and Git traffic. Review the provider, Coder and GitHub data paths before you deploy on sensitive repositories.

title: Can I run OpenFlows on a private repository?
summary: Yes, when the GitHub App installation has access to that repository. Manager checks that the repository belongs to the tenant's organization and brokers short-lived, scoped…
text: Yes, when the GitHub App installation has access to that repository. Manager checks that the repository belongs to the tenant's organization and brokers short-lived, scoped installation tokens. Human GitHub OAuth is used to sign in, not as the runtime Git token.

title: How does an agent act inside a workspace?
summary: Each agent runs in its own isolated, disposable Coder workspace. It registers with Manager, uses tenant-scoped runtime credentials and exchanges task messages with Nexus through…
text: Each agent runs in its own isolated, disposable Coder workspace. It registers with Manager, uses tenant-scoped runtime credentials and exchanges task messages with Nexus through the hook and A2A path. Its authority is limited to its tenant, workspace, repository and purpose.

title: How does SENTINEL decide whether to approve work?
summary: SENTINEL checks the work for security holes, quality issues and missing tests against the agreed plan. It reviews from its own workspace and never touches the builder's files.…
text: SENTINEL checks the work for security holes, quality issues and missing tests against the agreed plan. It reviews from its own workspace and never touches the builder's files. When it needs proof, it asks for an allowlisted command to be run in FORGE's workspace. When in doubt, it does not approve.

title: Can I run OpenFlows air-gapped or on-premises?
summary: You can self-host Manager, PostgreSQL, Redis and Coder on your own infrastructure. The GitHub integration needs network access to GitHub for OAuth, App installation, webhooks and…
text: You can self-host Manager, PostgreSQL, Redis and Coder on your own infrastructure. The GitHub integration needs network access to GitHub for OAuth, App installation, webhooks and API calls, so a fully air-gapped deployment is not supported today.

title: What happens if work gets stuck or fails?
summary: A reconciliation loop re-reads the system on a steady cadence, advances every ticket and repairs what it can, with a limited number of retries. When retries run out, the ticket is…
text: A reconciliation loop re-reads the system on a steady cadence, advances every ticket and repairs what it can, with a limited number of retries. When retries run out, the ticket is parked and escalated to a human with a notification, instead of failing silently.

title: What happens when there are merge conflicts?
summary: VESSEL watches CI and detects conflicts early. Fixable conflicts go back to the same FORGE worker with its context intact. A conflict that cannot be resolved is escalated to a…
text: VESSEL watches CI and detects conflicts early. Fixable conflicts go back to the same FORGE worker with its context intact. A conflict that cannot be resolved is escalated to a human.

title: Can several workers run at once?
summary: Yes. The agent registry sets how many workers a role may run at once. OpenFlows runs a fleet of worker workspaces in parallel and assigns work to whichever one is free.
text: Yes. The agent registry sets how many workers a role may run at once. OpenFlows runs a fleet of worker workspaces in parallel and assigns work to whichever one is free.

title: What happens to workspaces after a task?
summary: Worker workspaces are short-lived. They are provisioned when work is assigned and can be torn down when no longer needed. Tokens expire or rotate; verify workspace teardown and…
text: Worker workspaces are short-lived. They are provisioned when work is assigned and can be torn down when no longer needed. Tokens expire or rotate; verify workspace teardown and credential revocation in your own operations.

title: How do I change the configuration or add a skill?
summary: Adding a skill, connecting an MCP server or enabling another model is a configuration change in the agent registry, with no restart. Adding a brand-new role is the one change that…
text: Adding a skill, connecting an MCP server or enabling another model is a configuration change in the agent registry, with no restart. Adding a brand-new role is the one change that touches the code. See the guides .
